meta.blurb: A woman is attacked in a room with one locked door, one barred window and no chimney. Yet the attacker has vanished. Eighteen-year-old reporter Joseph Rouletabille says the answer is simple, if you take the puzzle by the right end.
meta.bible: Joseph Rouletabille: an eighteen-year-old reporter on the Epoque, round-headed, always smoking a pipe, who solves the case by taking his reason by the right end. Sainclair: his friend, a young lawyer, who tells the story. Professor Stangerson: a famous scientist who works on the Dissociation of Matter. Mathilde Stangerson: his daughter, aged thirty-five, who works with him. Robert Darzac: Mathilde's fiancé, a professor at the Sorbonne, who keeps a strange silence. Daddy Jacques: the old servant of the Stangersons, with a white beard and a Basque cap. Bernier: the gate-keeper, and his wife Madame Bernier, who poach rabbits. Frédéric Larsan: the famous detective of the Sûreté, also called Fred, who carries a yellow cane; in truth he is the criminal Ballmeyer. Monsieur de Marquet: the examining magistrate, who secretly writes plays. Monsieur Maleine: his registrar. Monsieur Dax: Chief of the Sûreté. Arthur Rance: an American from Philadelphia, a friend of the Stangersons, who drinks too much. The Green Man: the forest-keeper, handsome, dressed in green velvet. Daddy Mathieu: the bad-tempered landlord of the Donjon Inn. Madame Mathieu: his gentle wife. Mother Angenoux: an old woman of the forest, with a huge cat called the Bête du bon Dieu. Maître Henri Robert: Darzac's lawyer. Monsieur de Rocouz: the president of the court. The Yellow Room: Mathilde's small bedroom in the pavilion, with one door and one barred window. Château du Glandier: the old château in the forest near Epinay-sur-Orge, south of Paris. Paris. Versailles: where the trial is held. Philadelphia. Louisville. Cincinnati. America. Sorbonne. Élysée. The presbytery has lost nothing of its charm, nor the garden its brightness: the sentence that frightens Darzac and Mathilde. The perfume of the lady in black: Rouletabille's memory from childhood. Voice and tone: lively, clever and full of surprises, told by a friend who admires the young hero; the crime is stated plainly, without gore; the solution is simple and fair, and the secret is treated gently. Added for the full-length version: The Pavilion: the small white house in the park where the laboratory, the hall and the Yellow Room are. The Laboratory: Stangerson's workroom, with the great iron cabinet that holds twenty years of his papers. Jean Roussel: the name Ballmeyer used in Louisville when he married Mathilde. Palace of Justice: the law courts in Paris. Louisville: where Mathilde lived as Roussel's wife, in a little house called the Presbytery. The Presbytery: that little house. The Orge: the river near Epinay. The Galleries: the two long galleries of the château that meet at a corner.

A1A2: On a cold night in October 1892, a terrible crime shocked all of Paris.
The Château du Glandier was a lonely old house in a big dark forest.
Professor Stangerson and his daughter Mathilde worked together on important science.
Their laboratory stood in a small white house in the park.
At midnight, Mathilde said good night to her father and old Daddy Jacques.
She went into her little room, locked the door and pushed the bolt.
Half an hour later, Mathilde cried for help, and two shots rang out.
Stangerson pushed hard on the door, and old Jacques ran to get help.
Jacques came back with Bernier and his wife, but the cries had stopped.
They broke down the door and found Mathilde on the floor, badly hurt.
On the wall, there was a red mark of a big bloody hand.
On the floor lay an old cap, a revolver, a big bone and some boot marks.
They looked under the bed and behind the furniture, but nobody was there.
The door had been locked from the inside, and the key was in the lock.
The only window had iron bars, and the room had no chimney.
The doctors saw marks on Mathilde's neck and a bad wound on her head.
The servants said that only the Devil could do such a thing.
In Paris, a young lawyer called Sainclair read about the crime at breakfast.
Then his friend Rouletabille, a young reporter with a round head, ran into the room.
Rouletabille said that Mathilde herself had used the revolver, and he asked Sainclair to come.
At the station, Rouletabille said that he always starts at the right end of reason.
He saw the magistrate, Monsieur de Marquet, and his clerk getting on the train.
Rouletabille sat in their compartment and said he was a theatre critic.
The magistrate was proud and happy, and he said he wrote plays.
Slowly, the magistrate said that the revolver had not made Mathilde's wound.
The window in the hall had iron blinds, but there was blood on it.
Rouletabille asked how Mathilde wore her hair, and the answer made him sad.
At Epinay, a carriage took them toward the Glandier through the autumn woods.
At the park gate, they met the famous detective Larsan, who held a yellow cane.
Darzac arrived, and Rouletabille spoke strange words, so Darzac went white and let them in.
Darzac led them to the pavilion, a small white house at the end of the park.
In the hall, Rouletabille got down on the tiles and found one drop of blood.
Daddy Jacques said he washed the floor that afternoon, and nobody wore boots there.
In the laboratory, Rouletabille looked at the instruments and the big iron cabinet.
He took off his boots and went into the Yellow Room in his socks.
He crawled on the floor and under the bed, looking at every board.
He knocked on the walls and the ceiling to find a hidden door.
He tried the window bars and the shutters, but nothing moved at all.
Then he said that the room had been closed like an iron safe.
Jacques said he kept his revolver in a drawer, and Mathilde had asked for it.
The magistrate and his clerk came to the pavilion, and Rouletabille listened closely.
Daddy Jacques told again about the cries, the shots and his revolver.
The magistrate arrested Bernier and his wife, because they were dressed at midnight.
The doctor said the magistrate could see Mathilde for only five minutes.
Mathilde said she had been afraid for some days, so she borrowed a revolver.
She woke in the night and found a man at her neck.
She shot at him twice, but she remembered nothing after his blow.
She could not say what the man looked like, so the magistrate left angry.
Darzac sat beside her bed and held her hand without a word.
Outside, Rouletabille told Sainclair that Mathilde had not told everything.
In the garden, Rouletabille found muddy marks of heavy boots under the window.
Beside them, he saw a second set of marks, narrow and neat.
He followed the marks across the park to a small lake.
At the lake, the heavy marks stopped, and neat marks and bicycle tracks began.
Larsan came, looked at the ground, and said two men had worked together.
Rouletabille said no, because the murderer had worked alone and changed his boots.
Larsan said the blood in the hall came from a bleeding nose.
Rouletabille told him not to make the facts fit his idea.
Darzac came along the path and looked at the neat marks, and his face went white.
The neat marks were exactly the size of his own boots.
At dusk, the two friends walked to the Donjon Inn, next to an old tower.
Daddy Mathieu, the landlord, was angry, but his wife was kind and gentle.
A handsome man in green velvet walked past the window, and Mathieu frowned.
Rouletabille said, quietly, that they would have to eat red meat now.
Mathieu did as he said, then whispered that the man in green was the murderer.
His wife shook, and she begged him not to say such things.
That night, many people met in the laboratory to hear what Larsan thought.
Larsan was calm, and he said the murderer had left by the door.
He reminded them that Stangerson had stood alone at the door for some minutes.
He said the professor let the murderer go, to avoid a scandal.
Rouletabille asked the professor if the door had opened while he was alone.
Stangerson raised his hand and swore, on his daughter's head, that it had not.
Everyone doubted the old man, but Rouletabille believed him.
In the hall, Rouletabille found boot marks and the mark of a parcel.
The professor opened his iron cabinet, but it was empty.
Twenty years of his work were gone, and only Mathilde had a key.
Rouletabille remembered a small notice about a lost bag with a brass key.
The notice sent him to a post office in Paris.
A clerk said that a lady had come for a letter there.
Later, the clerk said, a man very like Darzac asked for the same letter.
In a café, Larsan put a new yellow cane on the table.
Rouletabille turned the cane and saw the mark of a Paris shop.
Sainclair went to the shop and learned that a man like Darzac bought it.
Sainclair walked home alone, and he felt worried about Larsan and Darzac.
That evening, Rouletabille told his friend a story he had kept secret.
Before the crime, he went to a big party at the Élysée.
There he saw Mathilde in white, and he followed her into the garden.
Darzac met her under a lamp, and she read him a letter.
The letter ended with a sentence about a presbytery and a garden.
Darzac went pale, Mathilde cried, and Rouletabille left to learn what it meant.
On the second of November, Sainclair got a telegram that said come with two revolvers.
Sainclair put two revolvers in his bag and ran to the station.
Rouletabille met him on the dark platform and took him through the park.
As they walked, he told Sainclair about the night he lay awake.
He heard a soft step outside and got up without a light.
In the corridor, he found fresh muddy marks of boots on the floor.
Outside, a tall ladder stood against the wall under Mathilde's windows.
Rouletabille climbed the ladder slowly and quietly, one step at a time.
Through the window, he saw a man in a long coat writing at Mathilde's desk.
He slid down quietly to wake the men of the house.
The château had two long galleries that met at a corner.
Rouletabille put Larsan, Jacques and Stangerson at the ends of the galleries.
Then he climbed the ladder and went in through the window.
A man with a red beard jumped up and ran at the door.
The man ran into the gallery, and Rouletabille ran after him.
The other three men ran in, and all four were near the corner.
But at the crossing, the man with the red beard was gone.
They searched every door and every window, but all were shut from inside.
They looked behind the curtains and in the cupboards, but found nobody.
The four men looked at each other, and nobody knew what to say.
Then Mathilde came to her door and said she slept in the next room.
The letter on her desk was gone, and she said nothing.
Rouletabille wanted to save her without making her speak.
The man in green said that he saw no ladder.
At dawn, Rouletabille looked for the ladder, but it was gone.
He drew a circle on his forehead and said he must think calmly.
Rouletabille had the gate-keepers set free, so they could help him.
Bernier and his wife promised to serve him well.
He wrote a list of names and crossed out the innocent ones.
He told Sainclair that he and Larsan walked two roads to the same house.
That afternoon, Darzac begged Rouletabille to guard Mathilde through the night.
He had to go to Paris, and he was afraid of a new attack.
Rouletabille put his hand on his heart and promised to watch over her.
At the same time, Mathilde sent her nurses away.
Rouletabille smiled, because he knew the murderer would come now.
At six, from a hiding place, the friends saw Mathilde pour drops into her father's glass.
At dinner, Stangerson, Larsan, Rance, Rouletabille and Sainclair sat down together.
Arthur Rance drank too much and talked about his home in Philadelphia.
Larsan and Rouletabille both said that they had found their man.
Then Larsan held his chest and fell into a deep sleep.
Rouletabille sent Sainclair to hide in a dark closet beside the gallery.
Through a crack in the door, Sainclair watched the gallery in the moonlight.
The forest-keeper in green came out of Rance's room with a parcel.
He made signs from a window, but nobody answered him.
Sainclair went to find Rouletabille and found him fast asleep.
He could not wake him until he threw cold water in his face.
Then a terrible cry rang out through the house.
A man ran out of Mathilde's rooms into the court, and shots were fired.
Bernier fired his gun, and the running man fell at the corner of the building.
Everyone ran with lanterns to the place where he had fallen.
The lantern showed the face of the dead man: it was the forest-keeper.
Rouletabille looked at his chest and said that a knife had killed him.
Men carried the body into the lodge and covered it.
Upstairs, Mathilde lay in bed, badly hurt, with three knife wounds.
The stolen papers lay on the floor of her room.
The doctor said she would live, and Rouletabille was glad.
At dawn, Darzac ran in and cried that he was too late.
A railway worker said he saw Darzac at the Epinay station at half-past ten.
The magistrate asked why he had been there, but Darzac said nothing.
They arrested him while Mathilde cried out his name from her bed.
Rouletabille told Sainclair that he had to go on a long journey.
He gave his newspaper a sealed letter with the name of the murderer.
The newspaper must open it in court, if he did not come back.
Winter came, and Darzac sat silent in his prison cell.
On the fifteenth of January, great crowds came to the court at Versailles.
Monsieur de Rocouz was the president, and Maître Henri Robert defended Darzac.
Darzac stood in the dock, and he said nothing to any question.
Larsan told the court his theory of the crime.
The court waited for Rouletabille, but he did not come.
Then a young voice rang out from the back of the court: it was Rouletabille.
Rouletabille said that he could not name the murderer before half-past six.
He said that Madame Mathieu had met the forest-keeper in the tower at night.
She went secretly to the old tower to see him.
She called him with a cry like a cat, and people blamed Mother Angenoux's cat.
She was also the black shape that Daddy Jacques saw in the park.
At half-past six, Rouletabille put his watch away.
He named the murderer: Frédéric Larsan, but Larsan had already left.
Then he said that Larsan was really Ballmeyer, a great criminal.
Ballmeyer had escaped from the police many times, and changed his face and name.
The president rang his bell, and the crowd leaned forward to hear more.
Rouletabille put an iron peg on the table in front of the judges.
It fitted a hole under the terrace, and Larsan used it to climb up.
He climbed to the gallery window while the others carried the dead man.
Larsan had also put a sleeping drug in Rouletabille's drink.
Then Rouletabille explained the mystery of the gallery: the man could not have escaped.
So one of the four men who chased him must be the murderer.
In two seconds, Larsan pulled off his false beard and joined the chase.
Rouletabille showed a pair of eye-glasses, left in Mathilde's room.
Larsan loved Mathilde madly, and he found her lost key.
He opened the cabinet, took the papers, and later put them back.
Rouletabille said that the murderer was never locked in the Yellow Room at midnight.
The attack had happened at about six in the evening, when Mathilde went in alone.
The man was hiding under her bed.
Mathilde shot at him and hurt his hand.
He ran out through the hall window, and she shut it behind him.
At midnight, she dreamed of it, cried out, and hit her head on the table.
Larsan had stolen Jacques's boots and cap, and he had boots made like Darzac's.
He wanted people to suspect both men.
As a detective, he cleared one man before he accused the other.
Next day, Darzac was free, and Jacques was cleared, and Rouletabille was a hero.
On the night train, Rouletabille said that the lie about the cane should have warned them.
Larsan bought the cane because his hand was hurt.
Years before, in Philadelphia, Mathilde loved a Frenchman called Jean Roussel.
She married him in secret, against her father's wish, and they lived in Louisville.
One morning, the police came, and she learned that her husband was Ballmeyer.
Heartbroken, she went home to her father and told him nothing.
Later she heard that Ballmeyer was dead, and she promised to marry Darzac.
Then Ballmeyer wrote to her about the presbytery, their little house in Louisville.
He threatened her father's work, so she kept the secret to the end.
Mathilde got better, and two months later Rouletabille sat sadly, thinking of the lady in black.
B1B2: On the evening of the twenty-fifth of October 1892, the newspapers of Paris print the news of a terrible crime. A young woman has been attacked in a lonely château, and nobody can understand how it happened.

The Château du Glandier is an old grey house standing alone in a forest near the village of Epinay-sur-Orge. Professor Stangerson, a famous scientist, has lived there for many years with his daughter.

The professor and his daughter Mathilde are working together on a great scientific idea, the Dissociation of Matter. All of Paris follows their work with respect, although few people really understand it.
Their laboratory is not in the château itself but in a small white pavilion in the park. Mathilde sleeps there too, in a tiny bedroom that everyone calls the Yellow Room.
On the night of the twenty-fourth of October, Mathilde works with her father until midnight. Then she kisses him, says good night to old Daddy Jacques, and goes to her room.
Mathilde turns the key in the lock and slides the heavy bolt, as she has done every night for some time. Nobody knows why she has begun to take such care, and she has told no one.
About half an hour later, the two men in the laboratory hear a terrible cry for help, followed by two shots. At the same moment they hear furniture crashing to the floor.
Stangerson throws himself against the door, but it will not open, and the cries grow weaker. Daddy Jacques runs through the dark park to the gate lodge to fetch help, leaving the professor alone.

Jacques comes back with the gate-keeper Bernier and his wife, who are fully dressed although it is the middle of the night. By now the cries have stopped, and a heavy silence has fallen over the pavilion.
At last the four of them break down the door. They find Mathilde lying among the overturned furniture, badly wounded but still breathing.
On the yellow wall of the little room, the print of a large red hand stands out clearly. A stained handkerchief lies on the floor beneath it, and the whole room smells of blood and smoke.

There are other strange things on the floor: an old cap, a bone as big as a man's arm, and fresh marks of heavy boots. Daddy Jacques's own revolver is there too, and two bullets have been fired from it.

The four people look under the bed, behind the curtains and inside the cupboard, but they find nobody. They swear that no one has passed them in the doorway, because they have been standing there since the door broke.

The door of the Yellow Room was locked from the inside, with the key still in the lock and the bolt shot. Nobody could have gone out that way without being seen, and nobody could have locked it behind him.
The room has only one window, which is closed by shutters and protected by strong iron bars. There is no chimney either, and the walls are solid, so the murderer has not left by any of these ways.
The doctors find marks of fingers on Mathilde's throat and a terrible blow on her temple. They say that she is very weak, and they cannot promise that she will live through the night.
At dawn the servants whisper in the kitchen that only the Devil could do such a thing. In the forest, too, people talk about the huge cat of old Mother Angenoux, which cried that night so mournfully.

The next morning, in his little room in Paris, a young lawyer called Sainclair opens his newspaper at breakfast. He reads the story of the Yellow Room twice, but he cannot see how any man could escape from it.

Suddenly the door flies open, and his friend Joseph Rouletabille rushes in waving the morning paper. Rouletabille is only eighteen, with a round head and a pipe between his teeth, and he already writes for a great newspaper.

Rouletabille says that the revolver was used by Mathilde herself, and not by the murderer. Then he asks Sainclair to dress quickly and to come with him to the Château du Glandier, where the Epoque has sent him.

At the station, Rouletabille explains to Sainclair that his friends gave him his strange name because of his round head. He adds that he always begins at the right end of reason, and that this is the only secret he has.

On the platform he points his pipe at an elegant gentleman, who is about to board the train for Epinay. It is Monsieur de Marquet, the examining magistrate, and his clerk Maleine is following behind him.

Rouletabille steps into the magistrate's compartment, sits down opposite him, and pretends to be a theatre critic. Sainclair, who stays in the next compartment, can only imagine what kind of conversation begins.

The magistrate is delighted to speak to a critic and soon admits, in a low voice, that he writes plays himself. He talks proudly about his unfinished drama, and he has quite forgotten that he is on his way to a crime.

Little by little, Rouletabille turns the talk toward the Yellow Room, and the magistrate lets a few facts slip out. He says, for instance, that Mathilde's terrible wound was not made by the revolver at all.

He adds that the only window which is not barred, the one in the hall, has iron blinds that were still fastened on the inside. Yet blood on the window shows that the murderer must have left the pavilion that way.
Then Rouletabille asks, as if it were a small matter, how Mathilde had arranged her hair that night. He sighs with disappointment when he hears that it was drawn tightly back from her forehead.
At Epinay-sur-Orge the party takes a carriage, and they drive toward the Glandier through the autumn woods. The leaves are falling, the road is full of mud, and nobody speaks for a long time.

At the gate of the park, Rouletabille meets the famous detective Frédéric Larsan, who is carrying a yellow cane. Larsan greets him politely, for the two have met before, but he watches the young reporter with a small smile.

Robert Darzac, Mathilde's fiancé, comes down the path and frowns at the sight of a journalist. Rouletabille says a strange sentence about a presbytery, Darzac turns white, and without a word he lets the two friends in.

Darzac leads the two friends through the park to the pavilion, a small white house with a low door. Inside there is a hall with a tiled floor, the door of the laboratory, and the broken door of the Yellow Room.

Rouletabille kneels on the tiles of the hall and looks at them as carefully as a jeweller looks at a stone. After a minute he finds a single dark drop of blood and shows it to his friend without a word.

Daddy Jacques, a white-bearded old man in a Basque cap, tells them he washed the whole hall that afternoon. He swears that no one with muddy boots has crossed it since, for the tiles would show every mark.

In the laboratory Rouletabille walks slowly between the tables, the glass tubes and the strange machines. His eyes stop at the great iron cabinet in the corner, where the professor keeps the papers of twenty years.
Rouletabille takes off his boots and goes into the Yellow Room in his socks, so that he will not spoil any mark. He asks Sainclair to stay by the door and to say nothing, whatever he may see.

He gets down on his hands and knees and crawls across the floor, and then he slides under the little bed. He studies each board and each corner as though the room itself might whisper something to him.
Then he stands up and taps the walls, one after another, and he taps the ceiling with a long stick. He is looking for a hidden panel or a secret way out, but every sound is solid and dull.
He tests the iron bars of the window one by one, and he tries the shutters with all his strength. Nothing moves, and nothing has been cut, so the window has certainly not been used by anyone.
At last he sits down in the middle of the room and lights his pipe with a quiet smile. He announces that no secret way exists, and that the Yellow Room was as tightly shut as an iron safe.

Back in the hall, Rouletabille asks Daddy Jacques where he kept his revolver. The old man answers that it lay in a drawer in the laboratory, and that Mathilde herself asked to borrow it two days before.
The magistrate and his clerk arrive at the pavilion and start to question the people of the house. Rouletabille stays close to them, with his pipe in his mouth and his ears wide open.
Daddy Jacques, shaking, tells again about the cries, the two shots and the terrible minutes at the door. He admits that the revolver on the floor is his, and that he feels guilty for having lent it.

The magistrate orders Bernier and his wife to be arrested, because they were dressed in the middle of the night. Everyone in the district knows that the two of them poach rabbits in the forest after dark.
A doctor stands at the door of Mathilde's bedroom in the château and holds up one finger. He says the magistrate may see her for five minutes only, because she is still very weak.
Mathilde speaks quietly to the magistrate and the clerk beside her bed. She says that for some days she has been afraid of someone, and that is why she borrowed Jacques's revolver.
She says that she woke in the night, and that she found a man's hands at her throat. It was dark, she adds, and she saw almost nothing of his face.
She fired at him twice, she says, and she has no memory of what happened after he struck her. Her voice is so low that the clerk has to lean forward to write her words.

The magistrate asks her to describe the man, but she answers only that he was tall and that she saw very little. He closes his notebook with an impatient shrug and leaves the room, plainly frustrated.
Robert Darzac sits at the head of the bed and holds her thin white hand in both of his. He says nothing at all, and she turns her face to the wall and weeps.
Outside, under the window, Rouletabille whispers to Sainclair that Mathilde has told them the truth. Then he adds, with a thoughtful frown, that she has not told them the whole truth.
Outside, in the garden under the pavilion window, Rouletabille finds deep muddy prints of heavy boots. He bends over them with a small notebook and measures each one carefully.
Beside them he finds a second line of prints, narrow and neat, which seem to belong to a different man. He says nothing to Sainclair and simply marks the place with two small sticks.
He follows the tracks across the park, over the wet grass and along a path that bends toward a marshy lake. Sainclair, who is already tired, hurries after him through the cold and the mist.
At the edge of the lake the heavy boot prints suddenly stop, as if the man had vanished into the water. A few steps further, neat prints begin, and beside them run the thin tracks of a bicycle.
Larsan arrives, studies the ground with his usual calm, and walks round the prints twice. He says that two different men must have worked together, one in heavy boots and one in neat ones.
Rouletabille shakes his head, and says that the murderer had no accomplice at all. He believes that one man simply took off his heavy boots, put on neat ones and rode away on a bicycle.
Larsan points his yellow cane at a dark stain and says that the blood in the hall came from a simple nosebleed. In his opinion it has nothing to do with any wound on Mathilde's body.

Rouletabille wags a finger at the detective and says, politely, that a clever man must never fit the facts to his idea. He says that the facts must come first, and that the idea must follow them like a servant.
Robert Darzac comes along the path and stops beside the lake, where he stares at the neat prints in the mud. His face turns as white as paper, and his hands begin to shake.
He lifts one boot and holds it beside a print, and the two match exactly. Everyone turns and looks at him, but he says nothing, and the silence seems to grow heavier every second.

At dusk Rouletabille and Sainclair walk to the Donjon Inn, which takes its name from the ruined tower beside it. A faint light shines in its small windows, and smoke rises from the chimney into the grey sky.

Daddy Mathieu, the landlord, is a bad-tempered man who grumbles at everything, but his wife is gentle and kind. She puts two glasses on the table and smiles shyly, while her husband stares at the two strangers.

Through the window they see a handsome man in green velvet walking slowly along the road. Mathieu scowls and mutters under his breath, and Rouletabille notices how quickly the landlord's face changes.
Rouletabille puts down his pipe and announces, in a quiet voice, that they will have to eat red meat now. Sainclair does not understand what he means, but the landlord seems to understand perfectly.

Mathieu obeys at once, and when he brings the plates he bends over the table and speaks in a hiss. He says that the forest-keeper in green is the murderer, and that everybody in the district knows it.
Madame Mathieu stands by the stove with her hands shaking on a tray of plates. She begs her husband not to speak like that, because no one can be sure, and a man's name is easily ruined.

That night the officials and the servants gather in the laboratory of the pavilion, because Larsan wishes to speak to them. The lamps burn low, and the great iron cabinet casts a long shadow across the floor.

Larsan stands calmly by the cabinet with his yellow cane in his hand, and he explains his theory slowly. In his opinion the murderer was never locked in the Yellow Room, because he left it by the door.

He reminds the company that Professor Stangerson stood alone before that door for several minutes, while Daddy Jacques ran to fetch help. Nobody, he says, can swear what happened in those minutes, except the professor himself.

Every face turns toward the white-bearded old man, who sits stiffly in the lamplight with his hands on his knees. Larsan suggests, quietly, that the professor opened the door for the murderer to avoid a scandal.

Rouletabille steps forward and asks the old professor, very respectfully, whether the door of the Yellow Room ever opened while he was alone before it. The whole laboratory holds its breath while it waits for his answer.

Stangerson raises his right hand and swears, by the head of his daughter, that the door never opened for a moment. He swears also that he does not know who the murderer is, and his voice does not shake.

The officials exchange doubtful glances, and the magistrate coughs behind his hand, for nobody believes an old man's oath against so clear a theory. Only Rouletabille looks at the professor with real trust.

Later, in the hall of the pavilion, Rouletabille finds boot marks on the tiles and, beside them, the clear mark of a parcel. Someone has set a package down there, and then picked it up again and carried it away.

The professor goes to his great iron cabinet to look at his papers, and he unlocks it with a trembling hand. He pulls the heavy door open and stares into the empty shelves, and the blood drains from his face.
The work of twenty years has disappeared, every page of it. Only his daughter Mathilde kept a key to the cabinet, and she lies upstairs in her bed, too ill to be questioned.

That evening Rouletabille remembers a small notice that he has read in a newspaper about a lost bag with a brass key. He wonders whether it can possibly matter, and the more he thinks, the more it seems that it must.
The notice sends him to a post office in Paris, and Sainclair goes with him. Rouletabille asks a clerk behind the counter a few quiet questions, and then he waits patiently for the answers.

The clerk remembers that a lady came to the counter some days earlier, and that she asked for a letter which was waiting there. She was nervous, he says, and she kept her veil down and left in a great hurry.

The clerk adds that a man came later to ask for the very same letter, and that he was very like Monsieur Darzac. Sainclair turns pale, and Rouletabille only taps his pipe against the counter and says nothing.
In a busy café, Larsan lays a new yellow cane on the table beside his coffee. He says, with a smile, that it comes from London, and that there is no other like it in Paris.
Rouletabille picks up the cane, as if to admire it, and turns it over in his hands. Underneath the handle he sees the small mark of a shop in Paris, and he puts the cane back without a word.
The next morning Sainclair goes to the shop and asks the owner a few careful questions. The owner remembers selling the cane on the evening of the crime, to a man very like Darzac.
Troubled, Sainclair walks home alone through the lamplit streets. He cannot understand why Larsan has told a lie, and he cannot stop wondering why Darzac's shadow keeps falling across the case.

That evening, by the light of a lamp, Rouletabille tells his friend something that he has kept to himself for weeks. It happened before the crime, he says, and at the time he did not understand its meaning.

He had gone as a reporter to a great reception at the Élysée, where the best of Paris society was gathered. Among the guests were Mathilde Stangerson and Robert Darzac, who stood a little apart from the crowd.
Rouletabille saw Mathilde, dressed in white, slip quietly out of the room and cross the lawn into the garden. He followed at a distance, because a good reporter must always be curious.
Darzac was waiting for her on a bench under a lamp, and they spoke for a moment in low voices. Then Mathilde took a letter from her bag and began to read it to him.

From behind a tall bush Rouletabille heard the end of the letter, and it finished with a strange sentence. It said that the presbytery had lost nothing of its charm, nor the garden anything of its brightness.
Darzac turned as white as the paper in her hand, and Mathilde began to weep without a sound. Rouletabille slipped away through the shadows, determined to discover what that sentence meant.

On the second of November a telegram from Rouletabille reaches Sainclair at his breakfast table. It tells him to come to the Glandier at once, and to bring two revolvers, because the murderer will come that very evening.
Sainclair puts down his coffee, takes his two old revolvers from a drawer and loads them with care. Then he packs a small bag and hurries to the station without waiting to finish his breakfast.

On the dark platform at Epinay, a round-headed young man is waiting for him, with his pipe glowing in the dusk. Rouletabille takes his friend by the arm and leads him quickly through the park toward the château.
As they walk in the dark, Rouletabille tells Sainclair what has happened since they last met. He begins with the night of the twenty-ninth of October, when he had a room in the château itself.
That night he lay awake in his bed, listening to the old house creak. After a while he heard a soft step in the corridor, and he rose at once without lighting his lamp.
In the corridor, he found fresh muddy prints on the polished floor, and they led toward the rooms of Mathilde Stangerson. They were the prints of a pair of boots, and they were still damp.
He opened a window at the end of the corridor and looked down into the courtyard. A tall ladder was leaning against the wall of the château, just beneath the windows of Mathilde's rooms.
Rouletabille climbed down to the courtyard and then went up the ladder very slowly, one rung at a time. He took care not to make a sound, because he knew that someone might be waiting above.
When his eyes came level with the window, he saw a light burning inside, and he stopped climbing at once. A candle was burning in Mathilde's sitting room, and the curtain was not quite closed.

At the desk, in the candlelight, a man in a long stooping coat was writing busily. His back was turned to the window, and Rouletabille could not see his face, but he saw that his hand was very steady.
The rooms of the château open onto two long galleries, which meet at a corner like the arms of a letter. A man who runs along one gallery must pass the corner, or else leave by a door.
Rouletabille quickly wakes Larsan, Daddy Jacques and Professor Stangerson. He posts them at the ends of the two galleries, so that nobody can escape without being seen.
Then he goes back to the courtyard, climbs the ladder again and enters Mathilde's sitting room through the open window. His heart is beating so loudly that he is afraid the man will hear it.
The man at the desk stands up and turns, and Rouletabille sees a thick red beard and a pair of wild eyes. Before the reporter can speak, the man rushes at the door and tears it open.
The red-bearded man bursts into the gallery and runs along it with all his strength. Rouletabille is a few steps behind him, shouting to the others to stop him.
Larsan, Jacques and the professor all hear the cry and begin to run toward the crossing of the galleries. In a few seconds the four men are drawing close to the corner from every side.
At the crossing, where they all meet, there is only an empty gallery. The man with the red beard has vanished, and not one of them has seen where he went.

They search with lanterns, one door after another and one window after another, but every one is closed and bolted on the inside. The floor is solid, the walls are plain, and the ceiling is high above their heads.
They pull back every curtain and open every cupboard and chest in the gallery, but nothing is hidden anywhere. There is no way out, and there is no trace of the man at all.
The four men look at one another in the lamplight, and each swears that he has seen nothing. The old professor trembles from head to foot, for the mystery of the Yellow Room has found a twin.
Then Mathilde appears at her door, pale and trembling, held in her father's arms. She says that she was sleeping in the boudoir, with her two nurses beside her.
Rouletabille goes into her sitting room and looks at the desk. The letter that was lying there has disappeared, and Mathilde says nothing about it when they ask.
She stands in the doorway with her eyes lowered, and the old professor holds her tightly. Rouletabille looks at her sadly, for he longs to save her without ever making her speak.
In the courtyard the forest-keeper in green, who has run up at the noise, says calmly that he saw no ladder. His face shows no surprise, and his green velvet is perfectly clean.
At dawn Rouletabille goes down to the courtyard to look at the ladder again. It is gone, and not even a mark in the earth shows where it stood.
He walks up and down the garden path with his pipe in his mouth. Then he traces a circle on his forehead with one finger and says that he must retreat into the circle of his reason.
Within that circle, he explains to Sainclair, no feeling is allowed, and only logic can enter. He then asks that the poaching gate-keepers be freed, so that they can be his helpers.
The magistrate agrees at last, and the Berniers walk out of prison blinking in the light. They thank the young reporter and promise to serve him faithfully, for he alone has believed in them.
In his notebook Rouletabille writes the name of everyone who lives or works at the Glandier. Slowly he crosses out each person who could not possibly be the murderer, and few names remain.
Late that night he sits on a stone bench in the dark, smoking his pipe. He tells Sainclair that he and Larsan are walking along two different roads, but both are heading toward the same house.
That afternoon Robert Darzac takes Rouletabille aside in the hall of the château and speaks in a low and anxious voice. He begs the young reporter to guard Mathilde through the coming night.
He explains that he has to go to Paris on urgent business, but he is afraid that another attack will come. When Rouletabille asks him who the murderer is, he shakes his head and will not say a word.
Rouletabille puts his hand on his heart and promises that nothing will happen to Mathilde while he is there. Darzac thanks him with a look of such gratitude that the boy feels almost ashamed.
A little later, Sainclair sees two nurses leave Mathilde's bedroom with their bags in their hands. Mathilde has sent them away herself, and she has told them that she no longer needs them.
Rouletabille smiles at the empty corridor and rubs his hands together. If the nurses are gone, he says, then the murderer will certainly come tonight, because the path is clear.

At six o'clock, from a hiding place near the dining room, the two friends see Mathilde come in with a small bottle. She pours a few drops from it into her father's glass, quickly and secretly, and slips away.

At dinner five men sit down together: Professor Stangerson, Larsan, Arthur Rance, Rouletabille and Sainclair. The lamp shines on the white tablecloth, and the old professor, tired and silent, hardly touches his food.

Arthur Rance, the American, drinks glass after glass of wine and talks loudly about his home in Philadelphia. His face is red, his eyes are bright, and nobody can tell if he is a fool or a very clever man.
Larsan and Rouletabille look hard at each other across the table. Each of them says calmly that he has found the man, and neither will tell the other the name.
Suddenly Larsan clutches his chest, goes pale and sinks back in his armchair. Within a moment, to the horror of the guests, he has fallen into a deep sleep.
Rouletabille takes Sainclair to a dark closet beside the gallery and gives him a revolver. He tells him to keep still and to watch the gallery through a crack in the door.

Sainclair crouches in the closet for what seems like hours, with the cold iron of the revolver in his hand. Moonlight comes through the windows and lies in long white shapes on the floor of the gallery.
At last a door opens, and the forest-keeper in green comes out of Arthur Rance's room. He is carrying a parcel under his arm, and he looks carefully up and down the gallery.
The man goes to a window and makes slow signs with his hand toward the park. Sainclair waits for a reply, but nobody answers, and the keeper's face shows his disappointment.
Sainclair leaves his hiding place when the keeper has gone, and he hurries to find his friend. He discovers Rouletabille stretched out on a sofa, fast asleep, and he cannot wake him.
He shakes him and calls his name, but the reporter does not stir. At last Sainclair fetches a jug of cold water and throws it in his friend's face.
Rouletabille opens his eyes, and in the same moment a terrible death cry rings through the château. It comes from the direction of Mathilde's rooms, and it makes the two friends spring to their feet.
A man bursts out of Mathilde's rooms and runs across the moonlit court, with the two friends racing after him. Shots are fired, and the echoes bounce between the old walls.
The gate-keeper Bernier, who is watching from the corner of the building, raises his gun and fires. The running man stumbles, rolls over and lies still at the foot of the wall.
Everyone runs toward the fallen man, some with lanterns, some with torches. Their shadows leap across the walls of the château, and their voices echo in the cold night air.
The lantern shows the face of the dead man, and everybody gasps, because it is the forest-keeper in green. His handsome face is calm, and his velvet coat is dark with blood.
Rouletabille kneels beside the body and studies the wound with great care. He says that the keeper was killed not by a bullet but by a knife, which was driven deep into his heart.
Four men lift the body gently and carry it across the court to the gate lodge. They lay it on a bed and cover it with a sheet, and the old women of the house begin to pray.
Upstairs, Mathilde lies in her bed with three knife wounds, one in the arm and two in the side. A candle is burning beside her, and she is alive, though she is as white as the sheets.
On the floor of her room lie the stolen papers of the professor's iron cabinet, scattered like dead leaves. Someone has thrown them down in a hurry, and nobody can say why.
The doctor examines the wounds and says that she may live, if she is kept quiet and warm. Rouletabille, who has not breathed freely for an hour, promises that she will, and everybody believes him.
At dawn Robert Darzac rushes through the gate, white with fatigue and fear, and cries out that he is too late. Rouletabille takes him by the arm and tells him gently that Mathilde is alive.

A railway worker steps forward and says that he saw Darzac at the station of Epinay at half-past ten that night. He is quite sure of it, because the professor passed so close to him that he could have touched him.
The magistrate asks Darzac why he was at Epinay at that hour, so near the château. Darzac says nothing at all, and the silence in the hall seems to grow very heavy.
At last the magistrate gives a sign, and two gendarmes lay their hands on Darzac and arrest him. From her bed upstairs Mathilde hears the noise and cries out his name again and again.
A few days after Darzac's arrest, Rouletabille tells Sainclair that he has to go away on a long journey. He will not say where, and he will not say for how long.
Before he goes, he seals a letter and gives it to the editor of the Epoque. The letter names the murderer, and it is not to be opened until the day of the trial.
He says that the editor must open it in court only if he himself has not come back in time. Then he puts on his overcoat, takes his travelling bag and walks to the station.
Winter comes, with snow on the roofs of Paris, and the weeks go by slowly. In his prison cell Robert Darzac sits silent, and he refuses every visitor except his lawyer.
On the fifteenth of January great crowds press against the steps of the courthouse at Versailles. They have come to see the famous Darzac case, and the doors are guarded by soldiers.

Monsieur de Rocouz, a stern man with a grey beard, presides over the court, and the famous Maître Henri Robert speaks for Darzac. The courtroom is so full that people stand on the benches and in the doorways.
Darzac stands in the dock, pale and calm, and he refuses to answer a single question. He does not defend himself, and he does not explain, and the president grows angry.
The detective Larsan is called to give evidence, and he tells the court his theory of the crime. He speaks quietly and clearly, and every point seems to fall into place against Darzac.
The hours pass, and the court waits uneasily for the young reporter who has promised to come. Sainclair looks at the door a hundred times, but Rouletabille does not appear, and the clock ticks on.
Then, from the back of the crowded court, a young voice rings out clearly above the noise. Everyone turns, and there stands Rouletabille in a travelling coat, with his pipe in his hand.
Rouletabille raises one hand, and the court falls silent. He cannot name the murderer before half-past six, he says, and until then he must tell the story in his own way.

First he explains the mystery of the night noises in the park. Madame Mathieu, the landlord's gentle wife, secretly met the forest-keeper in the old tower at night, and in the crowd she begins to weep.

She slipped out of the Donjon Inn in the dark, wrapped in a shawl, and hurried across the fields to the tower. There she waited for the man in green, because the two of them had loved each other in secret.
To call him, she made a cry like a cat's, and people believed it was the cat of Mother Angenoux. So the mournful cry that had frightened the servants had come from a human throat.
She was also the black phantom that Daddy Jacques had seen in the park on the night of the crime. Rouletabille explains that this innocent secret has hidden a far more terrible one.
The hands of the clock move slowly toward half-past six, and the court waits with its eyes on the young man. At last Rouletabille takes out his watch, looks at it carefully and puts it away.

Then he turns toward the empty chair beside the witness stand and names the murderer: Frédéric Larsan. But the great detective, who has slipped out of the court, is no longer there to hear his own name.
Rouletabille says that Larsan is not Larsan at all, but Ballmeyer, the greatest criminal of the age. The court breaks into uproar, and the guards run toward the doors.
Ballmeyer, he says, has escaped the police many times, and has changed his face and his name as other men change their coats. He has used the Sûreté itself as a mask.
The president rings his bell again and again and calls for silence. Little by little the noise falls, and the crowd leans forward, eager to hear the rest of the story.
Rouletabille puts an iron peg on the table in front of the judges and asks them to look at it closely. It fits a hole that he has found in the wall under the terrace of the château.
Larsan, he says, used this peg like a step to climb up the wall to the terrace. From the terrace he could reach the gallery window without ever being seen from the court.

He did it on the last night, while everyone else was running about with lanterns and carrying the keeper's body. In all that confusion nobody noticed that the great detective was missing for several minutes.

Larsan had also slipped a sleeping drug into Rouletabille's drink at dinner, and he had only pretended to fall asleep himself. That is why the young reporter could not be woken until Sainclair threw cold water over him.

Rouletabille now explains the mystery of the gallery, which has puzzled everybody for weeks. He says that the red-bearded man could not have escaped, because there was no way out, and so he did not escape.
If he did not escape, he must still have been in the gallery when the four men met. That means that one of the four men who ran after him was the murderer himself.

In two seconds, as he turned the corner out of sight, Larsan pulled off his false red beard and hid it in his coat. Then he ran on and joined the chase as the fourth man, shouting louder than any of the others.
On a table in the court, Rouletabille places a pair of eye-glasses that were found in Mathilde's sitting room. They belong to Larsan, and they prove that he was in that room that night.
Larsan loved Mathilde madly, Rouletabille says, and he followed her in secret for a long time. He found a key that she had lost, and he used it to open the iron cabinet in the laboratory.
He stole the professor's papers, though he could not use them. Later, perhaps from remorse, he put them back on the floor of her sitting room, where they were found.
Rouletabille announces that the murderer was never locked in the Yellow Room at midnight. The mystery, he says, has been wrongly set from the start.
The attack, he explains, happened about six in the evening, hours before the cries were heard. Mathilde had gone into her room alone, while her father and Jacques were busy in the laboratory.
The murderer was hiding under the bed, with his heavy boots in his hand and his cap on his head. He waited until she was alone, and then he sprang out and seized her by the throat.
Mathilde, who had borrowed Jacques's revolver, managed to fire it and wounded his hand. That is why the red hand was printed on the wall.
The man fled through the hall window, leaving blood on its blinds, and Mathilde shut the window behind him. She said nothing to anyone, because she was afraid, and because she had a secret.
At midnight, alone in the locked room, she dreamed of the attack and cried out for help. In her sleep she overturned the table, and the revolver fired, and she struck her head on its marble corner.
Larsan, who wanted a victim, had stolen Daddy Jacques's boots and cap. He had also ordered boots made like Darzac's, so that his own tracks would point to two innocent men.
With the false boots he walked in the mud and left his neat prints beside the lake. He wanted the police to suspect both men, and he wanted to be the one who found the truth.
As a detective, he then cleared one man before accusing the other, so that nobody could say he had been unfair. It was a game of a master criminal, who used the law to play with the law.

The trial is adjourned, and the next day Darzac is set free and Jacques is cleared of all blame. Rouletabille, who is not yet nineteen, is the hero of the hour, and the crowds cheer him in the street.

That night Sainclair and Rouletabille ride back to Paris on a night train, and Sainclair soon falls asleep by the window. Before he does, Rouletabille tells him that the lie about the cane should have warned them.
Larsan, he says, did not buy the cane for show but because his hand was wounded and he needed it to lean on. It was the wound that Mathilde's bullet had made.

The secret of Mathilde Stangerson began years earlier in Philadelphia, where she lived with her father as a young girl. There she fell in love with a charming Frenchman called Jean Roussel, who spoke beautifully and made her laugh.
Her father refused his consent, because he had discovered that the man was a swindler. Mathilde ran away to marry him in secret, and the couple lived for some time in the town of Louisville.
One morning the police knocked at the door of their little house to arrest Roussel. Then Mathilde learned the terrible truth: her husband was not Roussel at all but the famous criminal Ballmeyer.
Heartbroken, she went home to her father, who never knew where she had been. She hid the truth from him and worked harder than ever, believing that work would make up for her disobedience.
After some years a rumour said that Ballmeyer was dead, and Mathilde dared to hope again. When she agreed to marry Robert Darzac, she told him everything, and he loved her all the more.

Then the man she thought dead came back into her life and wrote her a letter that ended with the sentence about the presbytery. That was the name of the little house in Louisville where they had lived together.
Ballmeyer threatened to destroy her father's life work if she married another man. Mathilde chose to suffer in silence rather than let the old professor learn the horrible truth.

Mathilde slowly recovers, and Robert Darzac, free and happy again, hopes that quiet nursing will give her back her peace. Two months later Rouletabille sits sadly on a bench in the Palace of Justice, thinking of the perfume of the lady in black.
C1C2: On the twenty-fifth of October 1892, the evening papers of Paris announced a frightful crime that had been committed in the night at the Château du Glandier. The victim was the daughter of one of the most respected scientists in France, and the doctors would not promise that she would live. Within an hour the whole city was talking of nothing else, and nobody yet guessed that it would prove to be the strangest riddle in the history of crime.

The Château du Glandier was a lonely old house of grey stone, half hidden by the trees of a great forest near the village of Epinay-sur-Orge, a few hours south of Paris. Its towers had stood there for centuries, and the peasants of the district still told stories of the ghosts that walked its corridors. Professor Stangerson had chosen it precisely for its silence, since he wished to be left alone with his work.

Stangerson was a famous scientist with a white beard and a gentle, absent-minded manner, and his daughter Mathilde, who was thirty-five years old, shared every hour of his labours. Together they were pursuing a theory they called the Dissociation of Matter, which promised, if it proved true, to overturn the science of their age. Paris followed their experiments with admiration, even though only a handful of specialists could say what the experiments meant.

The laboratory was not in the château itself but in a small white pavilion at the edge of the park, a little way from the main building. It consisted of a hall, a large workroom full of instruments, and a tiny bedroom where Mathilde slept when her labours kept her late. Because the walls of that bedroom were hung with pale yellow paper, the household had always called it the Yellow Room.

On the night of the twenty-fourth of October, father and daughter worked together until midnight, as they often did, bent over their instruments in the silent pavilion. When the clock struck twelve, Mathilde rose, kissed her father on the forehead, and wished a good night to old Daddy Jacques, the faithful servant who looked after the laboratory. Then she went into the Yellow Room, which stood just off the hall, and closed the door behind her.

The two men heard her turn the key in the lock and slide the heavy bolt, a precaution she had taken every night for some time without explaining it to anyone. Daddy Jacques swept the floor, the professor gathered his papers, and the pavilion settled into the quiet of a late hour. Nothing in that peaceful scene could have warned them of what was about to happen.

About half an hour later, the silence was torn apart by a terrible cry for help, a woman's voice shouting for help and for murder to be stopped through the closed door. It was followed at once by two revolver shots and by the crash of furniture falling, as though a violent struggle had begun in the little room. Stangerson and Jacques stood frozen for a moment, and then both of them rushed at the door.

The door held firm, for it was solid oak and locked from the inside, and while the two men threw their weight against it the cries from within grew fainter and then stopped altogether. Realizing that they could not break it alone, Daddy Jacques ran off through the dark park toward the gate lodge, calling for help as he went. Stangerson was left alone in the hall, listening in horror to a silence worse than any noise.

Jacques returned a few minutes later with Bernier, the gate-keeper, and his wife, both of whom were fully dressed, although it was the middle of the night. Their clothes would soon seem strange to the police, but nobody had time to think of that now. The four of them stood together outside the Yellow Room, listening, and heard only the faint sound of someone breathing very slowly.

With a heavy piece of wood used as a battering ram, the four people at last broke the door from its hinges and burst into the room. Mathilde Stangerson lay on the floor among overturned furniture, her nightdress torn and her face white, wounded but still alive. For a moment nobody spoke, and then the old professor fell on his knees beside her.

The first thing that struck the eye in the Yellow Room was the print of a large red hand on the pale wall, as if someone had steadied himself there with a bleeding palm. On the floor beneath it lay a handkerchief stained with blood, and a heavy smell of smoke from the revolver still hung in the little room. Everything else was in chaos, with the table overturned, the chairs thrown about and the bedclothes torn.

Among the wreckage lay an old cap, an enormous bone, Daddy Jacques's own revolver and several fresh marks of heavy boots that looked like a labourer's. The police would later study each of these objects for hours without being able to make them tell a single clear story. Together they seemed to belong to a visitor who had come in from the forest, yet nobody could say how he had entered.

The four people who had burst in swore to everything holy that nobody had passed them on their way into the room, and when they searched, they found that nobody was hiding there. They looked under the bed, behind the curtains, inside the cupboard and even behind the lamp, but the room was as empty as a drawer. The attacker, whoever he was, seemed to have melted away between one second and the next.

The door that they had forced had been locked from the inside, the key still turned in the lock and the heavy bolt shot home, so that no human hand could have secured it from the corridor. Had anyone left through that door, he would have had to pass the professor and Daddy Jacques, who had stood in front of it for the whole of the time. A locked door, in other words, was the first of the Yellow Room's riddles.

The room had only one window, and that was closed by solid shutters and crossed by iron bars so thick that nobody could have slipped between them. There was no chimney in the room at all, and the walls, which the police tapped from top to bottom, gave back the dull sound of solid stone. Door, window and walls were all sealed, and yet a man had been in that room and had somehow gone out of it.

The doctors who examined Mathilde found the dark marks of fingers on her throat, as though someone had tried to strangle her, and a heavy blow on her temple that had almost taken her life. They shook their heads gravely, for she had lost a great deal of blood, and they would not say whether she could live through the night. All around her bed, in the meantime, the whole household waited in frightened silence for the morning.

At dawn, the servants gathered in the kitchen and whispered to one another that no human being could have done such a thing, so that it must have been the Devil himself. In the forest the peasants shook their heads at the huge cat of old Mother Angenoux, which they called the Bête du bon Dieu and whose mournful cry had been heard that night. Superstition spread through the district like a fog, and the police had to work against it as well as against the crime.

On the morning after the crime, in a small apartment in Paris, a young lawyer called Sainclair opened his newspaper and read the story with a growing sense of wonder. He read it a second time, slowly, trying to picture the room and the locked door and the vanished man, and he could not understand how such a thing was possible. It was then that the bell rang, and without waiting for an answer his visitor burst in.

The visitor was Joseph Rouletabille, a boy of eighteen with a round head, bright eyes and a pipe that never seemed to leave his mouth, who already ranked among the cleverest reporters on the Epoque. He waved the morning paper at his friend and cried that this was the strangest crime in years, one worthy of the best brain in Paris. Sainclair, who loved him dearly, smiled and waited to hear what he would say.

Rouletabille declared, with a calm that surprised his friend, that in his opinion the revolver had not been fired by the murderer at all but by Mademoiselle Stangerson herself, who had wounded the man. Then he asked Sainclair to dress quickly and to come with him to the Château du Glandier, because the Epoque had trusted him with the case and he meant to solve it. There was something in his voice, half laughter and half command, that made refusal quite impossible.

At the railway station, while the crowd pushed past them, Rouletabille explained to Sainclair that his friends had nicknamed him after his round head. He added that he never trusted his feelings, because his only guide was reason, and that he always began at what he called the right end. Sainclair, who had heard the speech before, smiled and followed him down the platform.

Rouletabille suddenly stopped and pointed with the stem of his pipe at an elegant gentleman who was about to climb into a first-class carriage, followed by a thin man with a bundle of papers. The gentleman was Monsieur de Marquet, the examining magistrate charged with the case, and his companion was his clerk, Maleine. It took the reporter only a moment to decide exactly what he would do next.

Without hesitation Rouletabille entered the magistrate's compartment, sat down opposite him and introduced himself, to Sainclair's astonishment, as a theatre critic of a Paris newspaper. The magistrate bowed rather stiffly, while the clerk, who had settled in a corner with his notebook, seemed hardly to notice the new passenger. Sainclair found a seat in the next compartment and wondered anxiously what would come of it.

Flattered to meet such a person, the magistrate soon forgot that he was on his way to the scene of a crime, and he confessed with a modest blush that he himself wrote plays in secret. He spoke warmly of an unfinished drama in five acts, and Rouletabille listened with every sign of interest, nodding and encouraging him with small questions. By the time the train left the suburbs, the magistrate had come to regard the young man as an old friend.

Little by little, as the train rattled through the fields, Rouletabille steered the conversation toward the Yellow Room, until the magistrate was speaking about the case with a confidence he would have refused to any official. He let it be understood that Mathilde's wound had not been made by the revolver, since the bullets had been found in the ceiling, and that the weapon had therefore wounded nobody at all. The reporter's eyes brightened with quiet satisfaction behind a thick cloud of tobacco smoke.

The magistrate went on to explain that the only window in the pavilion which was not barred was the one in the hall, and that its iron blinds had been found fastened on the inside. At the same time, there was blood on that very window, and so it seemed that the murderer had passed through it, which was plainly impossible. Marquet confessed, with a worried sigh, that he had never met a case so full of contradictions.

With an innocent air, Rouletabille asked the magistrate how Mademoiselle Stangerson had worn her hair on the night of the attack, as though such a detail could matter to a theatre critic. When the magistrate answered that it had been drawn tightly back from her forehead, the young man sighed with disappointment, as if a hope he had cherished had been disproved. Sainclair, who could hear nothing through the wall, was left to guess what these sighs might mean.

At the little station of Epinay-sur-Orge, the party found a carriage waiting, and the magistrate and his clerk invited the two young men to share it. They drove for an hour through the autumn woods, where the wet leaves lay thick on the road and the branches dripped in the grey light. Nobody spoke much, for the sight of the forest made every one of them feel the heavy weight of the mystery ahead.

At the heavy iron gate of the park they met the famous detective Frédéric Larsan, a quiet grey-haired man with a yellow cane, sent by the Sûreté to take charge of the case. Rouletabille, who had known him for some years and admired him greatly, greeted him with the respect of a pupil. Larsan answered kindly, yet his eyes watched the young reporter with the wary look of a man measuring a rival.

Robert Darzac, the fiancé of Mathilde, a professor at the Sorbonne, came down the path from the château with a haggard face, and he frowned deeply at the sight of a journalist. Rouletabille then said a strange sentence, which he had heard on another occasion, about a presbytery that had lost none of its charm, nor its garden any of its brightness. Darzac turned as white as a sheet, and without a word he ordered the gate to be opened for both of the friends.

Darzac led the two friends along a gravel path through the park to the pavilion, a small white house with a low door that stood apart from the château among bare autumn trees. Inside, a narrow hall with a tiled floor gave access to the great laboratory on one side and to the Yellow Room on the other. The door of the Yellow Room, splintered where it had been broken in, hung from its hinges like a wounded animal.

Rouletabille dropped to his knees on the tiles of the hall and examined them as carefully as a jeweller inspects a precious stone, moving slowly from one corner to the next. After a minute, with a murmur of satisfaction, he put his finger on a single dark spot and showed it to his friend. It was a drop of blood, and in this clean white hall it seemed as loud as a shout.

Daddy Jacques, the old servant, a stooped man with a white beard and a Basque cap pulled low over his eyes, said that he had washed the whole hall that very afternoon. He swore that no one had crossed the tiles since in muddy boots, for the damp floor would have shown every mark. His honest, frightened face gave his words a weight that no oath could have added.

In the laboratory, a long room lit by high windows and crowded with tables, glass tubes and curious machines, Rouletabille walked slowly from one end to the other with his hands behind his back. His eyes came to rest at last upon a massive iron cabinet standing in the corner, where the professor locked away the papers of twenty years of labour. He looked at it for a long time, as one might look at a face that one meant to remember.

Rouletabille sat down on the tiles, pulled off his boots and went into the Yellow Room in his socks, so that no footprint of his own should confuse those of the criminal. He asked Sainclair to remain at the door and to say nothing, whatever he might see, and the lawyer obeyed with the curiosity of a man who is about to watch a conjuring trick. The little room, bright with its yellow paper, seemed to hold its breath as it waited for him.

Dropping on his hands and knees, the young reporter crawled across the floor of the room with his nose almost touching the boards, and then he slid on his back beneath the narrow bed. He studied each board and each corner as though the room itself might whisper something to him if he listened long enough. Sainclair, watching him disappear and reappear, could not tell whether the boy was a genius or a madman.

Standing up again, Rouletabille tapped the walls one after another with the knuckles of his hand and then reached up and sounded the ceiling with a long stick, searching for a hollow place, a hidden panel or a secret door. Each sound that came back was dull and solid, as though the pavilion had been carved out of a single block of stone. The architect who had built it, it seemed, had made no provision for mysteries.

He tried the iron bars of the window one by one and then the heavy shutters, pushing and pulling with all his strength, until the sweat stood on his forehead. Nothing moved, no bar had been filed, no hinge had been touched, and not one screw had been loosened. Whatever the criminal had done, he had certainly not passed through that narrow window.

At last Rouletabille sat down on the floor in the middle of the room, struck a match and lit his pipe, with the quiet smile of a man who has finished a long calculation. He announced to his friend that there was no secret passage and no trick of any kind, and that the Yellow Room had been as tightly shut as an iron safe. For a moment Sainclair thought he had gone mad, and then he understood that this was what made the problem so beautiful.

Back in the hall, with his boots on again, Rouletabille asked Daddy Jacques where he had kept his revolver on ordinary days. The old man replied, twisting his cap in his hands, that it had lain in a drawer of the laboratory table, and that Mademoiselle Mathilde herself had asked to borrow it two days before the attack. He had given it to her without a question, he added, because he would have given her anything.

The magistrate and his clerk reached the pavilion soon afterward and set about questioning every person in the household with the slow thoroughness of men who have seen many crimes. Rouletabille, who had been allowed to follow them because Larsan had spoken for him, stayed close at their heels, with his pipe in his mouth and his ears wide open. Nothing that was said escaped him, and, strangely enough, nothing that he heard seemed to surprise him in the least.

Old Daddy Jacques, trembling a little, told once more of the cries, the shots and the terrible minutes that he and the professor had spent at the locked door. He admitted, with tears in his eyes, that the revolver found on the floor was his, and that he would never forgive himself for having let it out of its drawer. The magistrate wrote everything down in his neat hand, without a word of comment or the slightest sign of sympathy.

The magistrate, who needed someone to suspect, turned his attention to the gate-keeper Bernier and his wife, both of whom had been found fully dressed in the middle of the night. It was known throughout the district that the two of them poached rabbits in the forest after dark, and the magistrate drew the worst conclusions. He ordered them arrested on the spot, and two gendarmes led them off protesting their innocence.

A doctor stood at the door of Mathilde's bedroom in the château and raised a single finger, warning the magistrate that he might see the patient for five minutes and not a second longer. He explained that she was still extremely weak, and that any shock might undo all the good of the night's care. The magistrate bowed and went in with his clerk, leaving the door ajar behind him.

Mathilde spoke so quietly, in a voice like a thread, that her listeners had to lean forward to catch every word. She told the magistrate that for some days past she had felt afraid of someone, though she would not say whom, and that this was why she had asked Daddy Jacques to lend her his revolver. It was the only weapon she knew how to use, she added with a faint smile.

On the night of the attack, she said, she had been awakened by a noise, and in the dark she had felt two strong hands close around her throat. She had seen almost nothing of the man's face, only a shape bending over her, and for a moment she had been unable even to scream. Then, with a great effort, she had found both her voice and her revolver, and she had cried out for help while she fired.

She had fired at him twice, she said, and she thought that she had heard him cry out, but she remembered nothing after that. A terrible blow had struck her head, the lamp of her memory had gone out, and the next thing she knew was the doctor's face above her bed. Her listeners sat in silence, for it was clear that she was telling them all that she could.

The magistrate asked her to describe her attacker as exactly as she could, but she answered only that he had been tall and strong and that she had seen very little. He closed his notebook with an impatient shrug, for he had hoped for a name or at least a face, and he left the room plainly frustrated. The clerk hurried after him with his papers, and the door of the sickroom closed softly behind the pair of them.

Robert Darzac, who had not left the sickroom for a moment, sat down at the head of the bed and took her thin white hand in both of his own. He said nothing, and she said nothing to him, but her eyes filled with tears as she turned her face toward the wall. It was clear, even to a stranger, that these two people shared a sorrow that neither of them was willing to name aloud.

Outside, standing under the window of the sickroom, Rouletabille whispered to Sainclair that Mathilde Stangerson had told the magistrate the truth. Then he added, with a thoughtful frown and a long pull at his pipe, that she had certainly not told him the whole of it. He promised himself that he would not rest, or even sleep, until he had understood everything that she had left unsaid.

Outside, in the soft earth of the garden beneath the pavilion window, Rouletabille found the deep muddy prints of heavy boots, which led away from the building toward the park. He bent over them with a small notebook and measured each print with the care of a surveyor, writing down every number. It was the first time since the crime that anyone had troubled to look at them with such attention.

Beside the heavy marks he found a second line of prints, narrow and neat, evidently made by a different pair of boots and, it seemed, by a different sort of man. He said nothing of this to his friend but merely marked the place with two small sticks, as a gardener marks the spot where he has planted seed. Sainclair, who saw nothing remarkable in the mud, watched him with growing respect and a good deal of curiosity.

He followed the tracks across the park, over the wet grass and along a narrow path between dripping bushes, until they bent toward a marshy lake at the lower end of the grounds. Sainclair, already weary, hurried after him through the cold and the mist, holding up the skirts of his overcoat. The lake lay grey and still, with a few reeds trembling along its edge.

At the edge of the lake the heavy prints came suddenly to an end, as though the man who had made them had stepped off the earth and vanished into the water. A few paces further along, however, the neat prints began, and beside them ran the thin double track of a bicycle that had been wheeled away across the grass. Rouletabille stood quite still, and for the first time that day he looked pleased.

Larsan arrived soon after, with his yellow cane under his arm, and studied the ground in his usual unhurried manner, walking twice around the prints with his head bent. He concluded that two different men must have worked together, one wearing heavy boots and the other wearing neat ones, and that the second man had waited here with his bicycle. His conclusion was reasonable, and it was also, as Rouletabille would later show, quite mistaken.

Rouletabille shook his round head and declared politely that the murderer had no accomplice at all, and that one man had done everything himself. He thought that the criminal had simply taken off his heavy boots at the edge of the water, put on a pair of neat ones, and ridden away on his bicycle. Larsan smiled as one smiles at a clever child who has not yet learned how the world really works.

Larsan pointed his yellow cane at a dark stain on the ground and remarked that the drop of blood found on the tiles of the hall had come from nothing worse than a nosebleed. In his opinion, he said, it had nothing to do with the wound on Mathilde's temple and might have been left by anyone at all. Rouletabille thanked him gravely for the idea, and stored it away in his memory.

Wagging a finger at the detective like a schoolmaster, Rouletabille said, very politely, that a clever man must never bend the facts to fit his idea but must always bend his idea to fit the facts. The facts, he added, ought to come first, and the idea should follow them like an obedient servant. Larsan inclined his head with a faint smile, though his eyes, as the lawyer noticed, had grown a little harder.

Robert Darzac, who had been wandering alone through the park, came along the path and stopped beside the lake, where he looked down at the neat prints in the mud. His face turned as white as paper, his lips parted as though he would speak, and his hands began to shake. The others watched him in puzzled silence, wondering what he could possibly have seen in those muddy marks.

Slowly, as if in a dream, he lifted one of his own boots and held it beside a print, and the two matched exactly, even to the shape of the heel. Everyone turned and looked at him, and Larsan's eyes narrowed, but Darzac said nothing at all. The silence between the four men beside the lake seemed to grow heavier and colder with every passing second.

At dusk, when the lamps were being lit in the village, Rouletabille and Sainclair walked together to the Donjon Inn, a low crooked building that took its name from the ruined tower standing beside it. A faint yellow light glimmered in its small windows, and a thread of smoke rose from the chimney into the darkening sky. It was the sort of place where one expects to hear a ghost story.

The landlord, Daddy Mathieu, was a bad-tempered man with a heavy jaw who seemed to grumble at everything and everyone, but his wife was a gentle, timid woman who smiled apologetically at the visitors.
