She set two glasses on the table and withdrew behind the counter, while her husband stared at the two strangers with open suspicion. The low room smelled of wood smoke and old wine, and a large clock ticked slowly in its corner.

Through the window of the inn they saw a handsome man in a suit of green velvet walking slowly along the road with a gun under his arm, and Mathieu's heavy face darkened at once. He muttered something under his breath, and Rouletabille, who missed nothing, noticed how quickly the landlord's expression changed. The man in green passed on without looking in, and soon the road was empty again.

Rouletabille put down his pipe, leaned back in his chair and announced in a casual voice that they would now have to eat red meat. Sainclair, who had been expecting a quiet supper, stared at him in bewilderment, for the remark seemed to belong to another conversation altogether. The landlord, however, seemed to understand perfectly, and his face took on a strange expression of respect and alarm.

Mathieu obeyed without a word of protest, and when he returned with a dish and set it on the table, he bent over the two young men and spoke in a hissing whisper. He told them that the forest-keeper in green, the handsome fellow who had just passed, was the murderer, and that everybody in the district knew it perfectly well. His small eyes shone with an old and bitter hatred as he spoke, and his hands were clenched on the tablecloth.

Madame Mathieu, standing by the stove with a tray of plates in her hands, began to tremble so violently that the china rattled against the metal. She begged her husband in a low voice not to speak so, since nobody could really be sure of such a thing, and a man's good name was easily destroyed. Her husband glared at her, but she lowered her eyes and said no more.

That night the officials and the servants of the Glandier were gathered in the laboratory of the pavilion, because Larsan had announced that he wished to explain what he thought. The lamps burned low, the glass tubes gleamed in their cases, and the great iron cabinet threw a long shadow across the floor. Rouletabille leaned against the wall in a dark corner, where he could watch every face.

Larsan stood quietly beside the cabinet with his yellow cane in his hand, and he presented his theory slowly, as a man lays out the pieces of a puzzle one by one. In his opinion, he said, the murderer had never really been locked in the Yellow Room, because nobody had ever proved that he had stayed there. The company listened in respectful silence, for the detective was famous throughout Paris for the patience of his method.

He reminded the company that Professor Stangerson had stood alone before the door of the Yellow Room for several minutes while Daddy Jacques ran to fetch help from the gate lodge. Nobody could say what had happened in those minutes, he continued, nobody except the professor himself, and the professor had never been willing to describe them. A deep hush fell upon the laboratory as he finished speaking, and nobody dared to look at the old man's face.

Every face in the room turned toward the white-bearded old professor, who sat stiffly on a stool in the lamplight with his hands on his knees and his eyes on the floor. Larsan suggested, in a voice so gentle that it was almost kind, that the professor had opened the door for the murderer and then let him go, in order to avoid a scandal. For a few seconds nobody moved, and the clock on the wall ticked loudly in the silence.

Rouletabille stepped forward and asked the old professor, with great respect but also with great firmness, whether the door of the Yellow Room had opened even for a moment while he stood alone before it. The whole laboratory held its breath, and the clerk's pen stopped scratching on the paper. Every eye in the room was fixed on the white-bearded face of the great scientist.

Stangerson raised his right hand and swore, by the head of his beloved daughter, that the door had never opened and that he had never left it for a single instant. He swore also that he did not know who the murderer was, and that he had no idea how the man had escaped, and his voice did not tremble. It was the oath of a man who had nothing to hide, or of one who hid it very well.

The officials exchanged doubtful glances, and the magistrate coughed behind his hand, for nobody present was ready to believe an old man's oath against so clear and tidy a theory. Larsan merely shrugged his shoulders, and the servants began to whisper quietly among themselves in the corners of the room. Rouletabille alone looked at the professor with real trust, and the old man saw it and bowed his head slightly in thanks.

Later, when the pavilion was quiet, Rouletabille examined the hall once more and found on the tiles the marks of boots and, beside them, the clear impression of a parcel. Somebody had set a package down there, perhaps for a minute or two, and had then picked it up again and carried it away into the dark. He looked at that mark for a long time without moving, as a man looks at a word in a language he is learning.

The professor went to his great iron cabinet to look through his precious papers, and with a trembling hand he unlocked it and pulled back the heavy door. He stared into the empty shelves, where the notes of his life should have lain, and the blood drained from his face, so that Sainclair feared he would fall. He did not cry out, and this silence, so calm and so complete, made the scene all the more terrible to watch.

The labour of twenty years, every page of calculation and every record of experiment, had been carried off, and Stangerson said in a faint voice that he was ruined. Only his daughter Mathilde had ever possessed a key to the cabinet besides himself, and she lay upstairs in her bed, too ill to be questioned. Rouletabille took out his notebook and wrote one word in it, underlined that word twice, and then put the book away again without a comment.

That evening, while walking in the park, Rouletabille remembered a small notice that he had seen in a newspaper about a lost bag with a brass key inside it, and he wondered whether it could possibly matter. The longer he thought about it, the more it seemed to him that it must, though he could not yet say why. At last he told his friend that they must return to Paris at dawn.

The notice led him to a post office in the heart of Paris, where he and Sainclair presented themselves at a window and asked to speak with the clerk who was in charge. Rouletabille put several quiet and perfectly polite questions, in the manner of a man who already knows the answers and wishes only to see them confirmed. The clerk, flattered by the attention of a journalist, was only too happy to oblige them with every detail he could remember.

The clerk remembered very well that a lady had come to his counter some days earlier to ask for a letter which had been waiting there, and he said that she had seemed anxious and nervous. She had kept her veil down over her face all the time, he said, and she had hurried away as soon as she had the letter in her hand. He could not describe her face with any certainty, but he remembered her gloves, and he remembered that they were of a pale grey colour and rather worn.

The clerk added, after a moment's thought, that a man had come to the same window a day or two later and asked for exactly the same letter, and that this man had been very like Monsieur Darzac. Sainclair turned pale at the name, while Rouletabille only tapped his pipe lightly against the counter and thanked the clerk with a smile. He said nothing more to the clerk, nor to Sainclair, until the two of them were out in the busy street and the door had closed.

In a crowded café near the railway station, Larsan laid a brand new yellow cane across the marble table, beside his cup of coffee. He remarked casually, with his quiet smile, that it had been bought in London and that there was not another like it in the whole of Paris. His voice was perfectly calm, and nobody at the neighbouring tables paid him any attention.

Rouletabille picked up the cane as though to admire the polish, and he turned it over carefully in his hands. Beneath the handle, almost hidden by the brass band, he noticed the small stamp of a Paris shop, which showed that the cane had been bought in Paris. He laid it down again without a word, and began to talk of something else.

The next morning Sainclair, who had been sent on this errand, went to the shop in question and put a few carefully chosen questions to the owner. The old man remembered the sale at once, and he said that the cane had been bought on the very evening of the crime by a customer who was remarkably like Monsieur Darzac. The lawyer thanked him politely and went out into the street, where he found that he was feeling suddenly and strangely cold.

Sainclair walked home alone through the lamplit streets, with his hands in his pockets and his thoughts in confusion, unable to decide what any of it could mean. He could not understand why a great detective should tell so useless a lie about a cane, nor why the shadow of Robert Darzac kept falling across the whole affair. The streets, wet with the evening rain, gleamed like long black mirrors beneath the pale light of the lamps.

That evening, by the light of a single lamp in his little room, Rouletabille told his friend something which he had kept to himself for weeks and had mentioned to no other person. It had happened, he said, before the crime itself, and at the time he had not understood the meaning of what he saw. He lit his pipe with a steady hand, and Sainclair settled back in his chair and prepared to listen to every word.

A few weeks before the crime he had gone as a reporter to a great reception at the Élysée, where the best of Paris society had gathered under glittering chandeliers. Among the guests were Mathilde Stangerson and Robert Darzac, who stood a little apart from the crowd, and he noticed them at once. They were not speaking, but their silence had struck him as strange, and he had never forgotten it.

After a while Rouletabille had seen Mathilde, dressed in white, slip quietly out of the great room and cross the lawn toward a dark corner of the garden. He had followed her at a distance, because a good reporter must be curious about everything, and he had walked on the grass so as to make no noise. The night was cold and clear, and the sound of the orchestra came faintly from the lighted windows behind him.

Darzac had been waiting for her on a bench under a lamp at the end of the path, and the two of them had spoken for a moment in low and urgent voices. Then Mathilde had drawn a letter from her little bag and, with a trembling hand, had begun to read it aloud to him. Hidden behind a tall bush only a few steps away, Rouletabille had listened with all his ears, and he had not moved a finger.

The end of the letter, which he remembered perfectly, had consisted of one strange sentence, saying that the presbytery had lost nothing of its charm, nor the garden anything of its brightness. It had sounded like the most innocent phrase in the world, a line from some country letter written by a vicar's wife. Yet as soon as Mathilde read it aloud, her voice had broken, and the paper had trembled so that she could hardly hold it.

Darzac had turned as white as the paper in her hand, and Mathilde, covering her face, had begun to weep without a sound, while he stood helpless before her. Rouletabille, feeling that he had seen more than any stranger had a right to see, had slipped away through the shadows of the garden. He had resolved, there and then, to discover what those few words could mean.

On the second of November a telegram from Rouletabille was placed beside Sainclair's cup at breakfast, and he tore it open with a feeling of dread. It told him to come to the Château du Glandier at once, to bring two revolvers, and to say nothing to anyone, because the murderer would come that very evening. He read it three times over before he fully understood that it was entirely serious, and then he rose.

Sainclair rose from the table, took two old revolvers from the drawer of his desk and loaded them with great care, although his fingers were not entirely steady. He packed a small bag, put on his overcoat, and hurried to the station without waiting to finish his breakfast. During the whole journey he sat looking out of the window at the grey fields, and thinking.

On the dark platform of the little station at Epinay a round-headed young man was waiting, with the glow of his pipe lighting his chin, and he seized his friend by the arm without any greeting. Rouletabille led him quickly out of the station and through the park, avoiding the main avenues and keeping to the shadow of the trees. They said very little to one another until they reached the high grey walls of the old château.

As they walked in the dark, Rouletabille told his friend what had happened since they had last been together, speaking quickly and in a low voice, like a man who has long been waiting to unburden himself. He began with the night of the twenty-ninth of October, when Professor Stangerson, who had grown fond of the boy, had given him a bedroom in the château itself. Sainclair, with his heart beating fast and his bag still in his hand, listened eagerly to every word.

That night, Rouletabille said, he had lain awake in his bed, listening to the old house creaking and sighing around him like a ship at sea. After a while he had heard, or thought he had heard, a soft step in the corridor outside his door, and he had risen at once without lighting his lamp. He had crossed the dark room on the tips of his toes, and he had opened his door without making a sound.

In the corridor he had found fresh muddy prints on the polished floor, and he had followed them with the tips of his fingers, along the wall, toward the rooms of Mathilde Stangerson. They were the prints of boots that had come in from the garden, and the mud in them was still wet. He had felt his heart beating hard in his throat as he followed them, and he had not dared to breathe aloud.

At the end of the corridor he had opened a window and looked out into the cold courtyard, where the moon lit up the stones. A tall ladder had been leaning against the wall of the château, just beneath the windows of Mathilde's private rooms, and no one had been near it. Somebody, he had realised with a shiver, must already be inside the rooms above, and must have used the ladder to reach them.

Rouletabille had let himself down into the courtyard and had begun to climb the ladder, very slowly, one rung at a time, his hands cold on the wood. He had taken the greatest care not to make a sound, for he knew that if anyone were waiting above he would have no way of defending himself. The ladder had creaked only once, and he had held his breath for a full minute afterward.

When his eyes had come level with the window, he had seen a light burning inside, and he had stopped climbing at once, holding fast to the ladder. A single candle had been burning in the little sitting room that belonged to Mathilde, and the curtain had not been quite drawn. Through the gap he had been able to see almost the whole of the room.

At the desk, in the trembling light of the candle, a man in a long stooping coat had been sitting and writing busily, his back turned to the window. Rouletabille had not been able to see his face, but he had seen that the hand which held the pen was very steady, and that the man was in no hurry at all. He had understood, with a sudden thrill of certainty, that he was looking at the criminal of the Yellow Room.

The rooms of the château opened onto two long galleries, one running along the front of the building and the other turning away from it, so that the two met at a corner like the arms of a letter. A man who ran along the first gallery had to pass the corner, or else go out by a door, and every door gave onto a room with barred windows. It was, as Rouletabille saw at a glance, an excellent place in which to catch a man who had no wish to be caught.

Rouletabille hurried through the dark house and woke Larsan, Daddy Jacques and Professor Stangerson one after another, and he whispered to them that a stranger was in the building. He posted them at the far ends of the two galleries, so that nobody could possibly pass without being seen, and told them to hold their places whatever they might hear. They obeyed him with surprising readiness, although Larsan raised his eyebrows and the professor looked quite frightened.

Then he went back down to the courtyard, put his foot on the ladder once more, and climbed again, and this time he went right up and over the sill into Mathilde's sitting room through the open window. His heart was beating so loudly in the silence that he was afraid the intruder would hear it, and he moved forward like a cat. The candle was still burning on the desk beside the open drawer, and the light of it shook on the wall.

The man at the desk rose and turned, and Rouletabille saw a thick red beard, a pair of wild eyes and a large pale forehead, all for an instant in the candlelight. Before the reporter could say a word, the man gave a cry, overturned the candle, rushed to the door and tore it open with a violent hand. Darkness filled the room, and the footsteps of the fugitive rang away down the long stone gallery toward the corner.

The red-bearded man burst out into the gallery and ran along it with all his strength, his long coat flapping behind him like the wings of a great bird. Rouletabille was only a few steps behind, shouting to the others to stop him, and the noise of their boots echoed from the old walls. The chase lasted only a few seconds, yet to the breathless young reporter it seemed to last for an eternity.

Larsan, Daddy Jacques and the professor heard the cry and ran toward the middle of the galleries, each from his own end, so that the four men were closing in on the corner from every side. The runner could not go back, and he could not go on without meeting someone, for the trap was now complete. Never, it seemed, had a net been spread so carefully and so quickly around a single man.

But when the four men met at the crossing of the two galleries, they found only an empty corridor lit by the pale light of a lantern, and silence. The man with the red beard had vanished like smoke, and not one of them could say where he had gone, though each had kept his eyes fixed on the very spot. Rouletabille stood quite still in the middle of the gallery, with his chest heaving and his eyes wide open in astonishment.

They searched at once, with lanterns held high, one door after another and one window after another, but every door was closed and bolted from the inside, and every window was locked and barred. The floor was of solid oak, the walls were plain, and the ceiling arched high above their heads without a hole or a trapdoor. Where, then, in the name of all reason, could the man have gone, and by what way had he left them?

They drew back every curtain, they opened every cupboard and every chest that stood in the gallery, and they even looked behind the old tapestries on the walls, but nothing was hidden anywhere. There was no way out of that place for a man or for a mouse, and no trace of the fugitive could be found. The silence in the long gallery grew heavier and more strange with each moment that passed, and no one dared to break it.

The four men looked at one another in the lamplight, and each one swore that he had seen nothing of the man's escape and could say nothing of how it had been done. The old professor trembled from head to foot and leaned against the wall, for he understood that the mystery of the Yellow Room had now found a twin. Nobody spoke for a long time after that, and the only sound was the slow ticking of a clock somewhere in the house.

Then Mathilde Stangerson appeared at the door of her rooms, deathly pale and trembling, supported in her father's arms, and the four men fell silent at the sight of her. She said in a faint voice that she had been sleeping in the boudoir next to her bedroom, with her two nurses lying beside her, and that she had heard nothing of the disturbance. Nobody who looked at her could say with any confidence whether she was telling the truth or hiding it.

Rouletabille entered her sitting room, with a candle in his hand, and went at once to the desk where the stranger had been sitting. The letter that had lain there, half written, had disappeared, and when he asked her about it Mathilde looked past him and said nothing at all. Her silence told him a great deal more than any words of hers could have done, and he did not press her.

She stood in the doorway with her eyes lowered and her hands clasped, while the old professor held her tightly as though he feared she might fall. Rouletabille, who had never before felt so strongly for another person, looked at her sadly, for he longed to save her without ever making her speak. He knew, however, that this would be harder than any riddle of locks and doors.

In the courtyard the forest-keeper in green, who had hurried up at the sound of the shouting, said calmly that he had seen no ladder at all against the wall. He was a handsome, quiet man, and his face showed no surprise whatever, while his green velvet was perfectly clean and dry. Rouletabille noted that he had arrived suspiciously quickly, and put the thought away for later.

At the first light of dawn Rouletabille went down into the courtyard to look at the ladder once more, and found that there was no ladder to look at. It had been removed during the night, and not even a mark in the earth showed where its feet had rested, as though it had been a mere dream of his own. He stood for a long while and stared at the empty ground, as though it might still be persuaded to speak.

He walked up and down the garden path for an hour, with his pipe in his mouth and his hands behind his back, like a man weighing a hundred objects in his mind. At last he stopped and traced a circle upon his forehead with one finger, and said aloud that he must retreat into the circle of his reason. It was an odd habit, which made the servants smile, and one that was to make him famous throughout all Paris.

Within that circle, he explained to the astonished Sainclair, no feeling or fancy was allowed to enter, and only the cold bright light of logic could shine. Having said this, he sent a message to the magistrate asking that the two gate-keepers be set free, since he proposed to employ them as helpers. The request seemed absurd to everyone who heard it, but, to the general surprise, it was granted within the hour.

The magistrate agreed at last, though grumbling, and the Berniers came out of prison blinking in the daylight, a pair of poachers with grey faces and rough hands. They thanked the young reporter with tears in their eyes and promised to serve him faithfully, for he was the only person in the world who had believed in them. Rouletabille put them to watch the park and the paths of the forest, and told them to report only to him.

In his notebook Rouletabille wrote the name of every person who lived, worked or slept at the Glandier, and he considered each of them in turn for a long time. Slowly, with his pencil, he crossed out each person who could not possibly have been the murderer, and few names remained. The pencil stopped again and again above the same few words, and each time he shook his head and went on.

Late that night he sat on a cold stone bench in the park, smoking his pipe and looking at the stars between the leafless branches. He told Sainclair, in a voice that was almost gentle, that he and Larsan were walking along two quite different roads, and that both of them were heading toward the same house. Then he stopped speaking altogether, and the night closed in around the two friends, cold and silent and full of unanswered questions.

That afternoon Robert Darzac took Rouletabille aside in the great hall of the château, and spoke to him in a low voice that trembled with anxiety. He begged the young reporter, whom he had come to trust in spite of himself, to guard Mathilde Stangerson through the coming night with all the care that he could command. It was a request that no man in his position could have made lightly, and Rouletabille understood this at once.

He explained that urgent business called him to Paris and that he could not put it off, but he feared that a new attack might come before he returned. When Rouletabille asked him the name of the murderer, whom he must surely know, Darzac shook his head with a despairing look and refused to say a single word. He seemed to Rouletabille like a man held fast by a chain that he could neither break nor show to anyone.

Rouletabille put his hand on his heart and promised, with a gravity beyond his years, that nothing would happen to Mademoiselle Stangerson while he was there to prevent it. Darzac thanked him with a look of such deep gratitude that the boy felt almost ashamed of the suspicions he had once entertained against the man. Then Darzac left the château in haste, and a few minutes later Sainclair heard the wheels of his carriage rolling away down the avenue.

A little later Sainclair noticed two nurses leaving Mathilde's bedroom with their bags in their hands, walking quickly down the stairs with downcast eyes. Mathilde herself had dismissed them, and she had told them that she no longer needed them, that she was quite well enough to be left alone. It seemed a strange decision for a woman who had so nearly died a week before.

Rouletabille smiled at the empty corridor and rubbed his hands together like a man who has been dealt a winning card. If the nurses were gone, he declared to his friend, then the murderer would certainly come that very night, because the path was clear and the hour was ripe. His eyes shone with the keen joy of the hunter who hears the first sound of the game among the trees.

At six o'clock, from a hiding place in a recess near the dining room, the two friends saw Mathilde come in alone with a small bottle in her hand and look anxiously around her. She poured a few drops from it into her father's glass, quickly and secretly, then slipped away again like a shadow. Neither friend dared to breathe or to move a finger until the sound of her footsteps had faded quite away.

At dinner five men sat down together at the long table in the dining room: Professor Stangerson, the detective Larsan, the American Arthur Rance, and the two friends, Rouletabille and Sainclair. The lamp threw a warm light on the white tablecloth and the silver, but the atmosphere was heavy, and the old professor, tired and silent, hardly touched his food. Nobody at the table guessed what the night would bring, and the clock on the wall struck seven without any one of them noticing.

Arthur Rance, an American from Philadelphia and an old friend of the Stangersons, drank glass after glass of wine and talked in a loud, rather thick voice about his home across the ocean. His face grew red, his eyes grew bright, and nobody at the table could tell whether he was a fool or a very clever man pretending to be one. Rouletabille watched him over the rim of his glass with the quiet, unblinking attention that he gave to everything in that house.

Larsan and Rouletabille looked hard at each other across the table, like two duellists measuring one another before the fight. Each of them said calmly, in a voice that carried across the room, that he had already found the murderer, but neither would tell the other the name. The others looked from one to the other, bewildered and a little frightened, and the professor's fork stopped halfway to his mouth.

Suddenly Larsan clutched at his chest, went deathly pale, and sank back in his armchair with a look of astonishment, as though some invisible hand had struck him down. Within a moment, to the horror of everybody at the table, he had fallen into a deep sleep from which no shaking or calling could rouse him. The old professor rose in alarm and sent a servant running to the village for a doctor, though nobody could find any cause for so sudden a sleep.

Rouletabille led Sainclair to a dark closet beside the long gallery, put a loaded revolver in his hand, and told him in a whisper to keep absolutely still and to watch the gallery through a crack in the door. He did not explain why, and he did not say what the lawyer ought to do if something should happen. Then he went away down the gallery without another word, closing the door of the closet softly behind him.

Sainclair crouched in the closet for what seemed like hours, with the cold iron of the revolver in his fist and his heart beating against his ribs. Moonlight came through the tall windows and lay in long white shapes on the floor of the gallery, and every small creak of the old house made him start. He tried not to think too closely of what he might be about to see, and he gripped the revolver tighter.

At last a door opened in the silence, and the forest-keeper in green came quietly out of Arthur Rance's room, looking carefully up and down the gallery before he moved. Under his arm he carried a parcel wrapped in dark cloth, and his handsome face was calm, though the moonlight showed a thin line of sweat on his forehead. Sainclair, scarcely breathing in his dark corner, watched the man tiptoe along the wall and pause by every door.

The man went to a window at the end of the gallery and made slow signs with his hand toward the dark park, as though he were signalling to someone waiting among the trees. Sainclair waited for a reply, but nobody answered, and the keeper's face showed plain disappointment as he turned away. He vanished into the shadows at the far end of the gallery with his parcel still under his arm, and the silence closed behind him.

When the keeper had gone, Sainclair slipped out of his hiding place and hurried through the house in search of his friend, whom he found at last stretched out on a sofa, fast asleep. He called to him in a whisper, then in a louder voice, but Rouletabille did not stir, and his breathing was heavy and slow like a drugged man's. It was clear to the lawyer, even in his confusion, that something was seriously and dangerously wrong in the house.

Sainclair shook him by the shoulders and called his name again and again, but the young reporter only murmured something and rolled his round head on the cushion. In despair, Sainclair ran to fetch a jug of cold water and threw the whole of it in his friend's face, and Rouletabille sat up with a gasp, spluttering. For a moment he did not know where he was or what had happened, and his round face wore a look of utter bewilderment.

Rouletabille opened his eyes, and at the very same moment a terrible death cry rang through the whole château, from somewhere on the upper floors. It came from the direction of Mathilde's rooms, and it was so full of pain and terror that both friends sprang to their feet with their hair standing on end. Rouletabille ran for the door, still wet from head to foot and half asleep, with Sainclair close behind him on the stairs.

They rushed down into the court and saw a man burst out of the building near Mathilde's rooms and run across the moonlit stones, and they raced after him. Shots were fired from somewhere in the darkness, the echoes bounded between the old walls, and the running man did not slow his pace. He ran like a man who had nothing left to lose, with his head down and his coat flying out behind him.

The gate-keeper Bernier, who had been placed by Rouletabille to watch the court, raised his gun at the corner of the building and fired once, with a poacher's steady aim. The running man stumbled, threw out his arms, rolled over twice on the stones, and lay still at the foot of the wall without any further movement. The echo of the shot died away slowly among the dark trees of the park, and an enormous silence followed it.

Everyone ran toward the fallen man at once, some with lanterns, some with torches, some with nothing but their bare hands, and their shadows leapt across the walls of the château like a crowd of giants. The voices of the servants echoed in the cold night air, and a dog began to bark somewhere beyond the park. Nobody yet dared to guess aloud whose body lay there, and the lanterns shook in the hands of the men who carried them.

The light of the lantern fell upon the face of the dead man, and the whole company drew in its breath at once, for it was the forest-keeper in green. His handsome face was calm, almost smiling, and his velvet coat was dark and heavy with blood that had soaked through to the stones. Nobody spoke at all, and in the heavy silence of the court the flame of the lantern trembled in its glass.

Rouletabille knelt beside the body and studied the wound for a long time with a steadiness that astonished the others, who looked away. He declared that the keeper had been killed not by Bernier's bullet but by a knife, which had been driven with terrible skill straight into his heart. The gate-keeper, who had been dreading a murder charge against himself, almost wept aloud with relief at these words.

Four men lifted the body gently and carried it across the court to the gate lodge, where they laid it on a narrow bed and covered it with a sheet. The old women of the household began to murmur their prayers, while the moon set and the sky over the forest grew slowly pale. It was the hour of the night when the darkness seems longest and coldest.

Upstairs, in the great bed of her room in the château, Mathilde lay with three knife wounds in her arm and her side, so pale that she seemed already dead, while a single candle burned on the table beside her. Yet she was breathing, and when Rouletabille bent over her he felt the faint warmth of her breath on his hand. Beside her bed, on the carpet, there lay a dark pool of blood, and the sight of it made even the doctor's hand shake.

On the floor of her sitting room lay the papers stolen from the iron cabinet, scattered about like dead leaves, as if someone had thrown them down in a great hurry. Nobody could guess why the thief should have brought them back, after taking such pains to carry them off, and Rouletabille looked at them with a long and thoughtful stare. He did not touch a single sheet of them, and he asked that nobody else should do so until the magistrate had come.

The doctor, who had been fetched from the village in the middle of the night, examined her wounds and said at last that she might live, provided she was kept quiet and warm and carefully nursed. Rouletabille, who had not breathed freely for an hour, promised that she would live, and in some strange way everyone present believed him. It was a promise that the young reporter had made in all sincerity, and he meant to keep it with all the strength that he had.

At dawn Robert Darzac came running through the gate of the park, white with fatigue and terror, with his hat gone and his coat torn, and he cried out that he was too late. Rouletabille met him on the path, took him gently by the arm, and told him that Mathilde was still alive. The man's knees gave way, and he had to sit down on a stone.

Then a railway worker, summoned by the magistrate, stepped forward from the little crowd and said loudly that he had seen Monsieur Darzac at the station of Epinay at half-past ten that night. He was perfectly sure of it, he said, because the gentleman had passed so close to him that he could have touched his sleeve. Every head turned toward Darzac, and the pale man on the stone seemed to shrink beneath their eyes.

The magistrate, in a cold voice, asked Darzac to explain why he had been at Epinay at that hour, so near the château, when he was supposed to be in Paris. Darzac looked at him with sad, steady eyes and said nothing at all, not even a word of denial. It was the silence of a man who had made up his mind never to speak, and it grew heavier with every moment that passed in the hall.

At last the magistrate made a sign, and two gendarmes stepped forward and laid their hands upon Darzac, who allowed himself to be led away without a word of protest. From her bed upstairs, Mathilde heard the noise and the heavy footsteps, and she began to cry out his name. Over and over she called it, in a voice so broken and desperate that it pierced the heart of everyone who heard it.

A few days after the arrest of Darzac, Rouletabille told Sainclair, in his usual calm and decided manner, that he must go away at once on a long journey. He would not say where he was going, and he would not say how long he would stay away, and nothing that his friend could say could change his mind. Sainclair gave up asking at last, with a weary sigh, and resigned himself to waiting for news that did not come.

Before he left, Rouletabille sealed a letter in a thick envelope and carried it himself to the editor of the Epoque, whom he trusted completely. In that letter, he said, the name of the murderer was written, and nobody was to read it until the day of the trial. The editor, who was greatly impressed by the boy's gravity, locked the letter in his private safe and promised to keep the secret.

He gave one further instruction: if he himself had not returned by the time the trial began, the editor was to take the letter to the court and open it there, in front of everybody. Then he put on his overcoat, picked up his small travelling bag, and walked to the station without once looking back. Sainclair watched from the doorway until the small grey figure with the round head was lost among the crowds of travellers.

Winter came down upon Paris, with grey skies and snow on the roofs, and the weeks went by slowly while nothing was heard from Rouletabille. In his prison cell Robert Darzac sat silent, refusing every visitor except his lawyer, and answering the questions of the magistrate with only a gentle shake of the head. It seemed to those who thought of him that he had been entirely forgotten by a world which had once admired and feared him.

On the fifteenth of January great crowds pressed against the steps of the courthouse at Versailles, where the doors were guarded by soldiers, and the people had come from all over France to see the famous trial. The case of the Yellow Room had become the talk of every dinner table, and everybody wished to see the accused. It was a cold and brilliant morning, and the sun glittered on the wet stones of the great square before the courthouse.

The president of the court, Monsieur de Rocouz, a stern man with a grey beard and a deep voice, took his seat beneath the painted ceiling, and the famous Maître Henri Robert rose to speak for the defence. The courtroom was so full that people stood on the benches and crowded the doorways, and the heat of so many bodies made the air heavy. Everyone in that vast and breathless crowd watched the dock, where the accused man was about to be brought in.

Darzac stood in the dock, pale and calm, with his hands folded, and he refused to answer a single one of the president's questions. He did not defend himself, he did not explain where he had been on the night of the murder, and the more he kept silent the more the president's patience wore thin. The crowd in the benches murmured with excitement and disappointment, for they had hoped to hear him tell a great story.

The detective Larsan was called to give evidence, and he laid before the court his theory of the crime, speaking quietly and clearly and without any note of triumph. Point by point, the prints in the mud, the cane, the letter at the post office and the visit to the station seemed to fall into place against the accused. His calm voice held every listener in the hall spellbound, and not even the clerks dared to cough while he spoke.

The hours passed, and the court waited uneasily for the young reporter who had promised to be there, while the clock above the president's head ticked loudly in the pauses. Sainclair looked at the door a hundred times, and the sealed letter in the editor's pocket seemed to burn a hole through the cloth. Rouletabille did not appear, and the president, glancing at the clock, began to prepare to bring the session to an end.

Then, from the very back of the crowded courtroom, a young voice rang out clearly above the noise and the shuffling of feet, saying that the court must wait. Every head turned, the guards moved forward, and there stood Rouletabille at the door in a dusty travelling coat, with his pipe in one hand and his round face flushed with haste. A great murmur of surprise and relief ran through the whole court, and Sainclair leapt to his feet with a joyful cry.

Rouletabille raised one hand, and the whole court, which had been buzzing like a hive, fell silent at once. He said in a clear voice that he could not name the murderer before half-past six, and that until that hour he must be allowed to tell the story in his own way. The president, who had expected a scandal, nodded gravely, and the clerks of the court bent over their papers again.

He began with the mystery of the night noises in the park, and he explained that Madame Mathieu, the gentle wife of the landlord of the Donjon Inn, had secretly met the forest-keeper in the old tower at night. In the crowd, a thin woman in a dark shawl began to weep, and her husband stared at her in horror. The story seemed to draw every person in the great hall closer together, and no one in the benches stirred or whispered.

She had slipped out of the inn in the dark, wrapped in a shawl, and hurried across the fields to the ruined tower, where the handsome man in green was waiting for her. The two of them had loved each other in secret for a long time, for her husband was a harsh and jealous man who would never have forgiven her. Rouletabille spoke of this love gently and without any scorn, and even the president lowered his eyes while he listened.

To call the keeper to the tower, Madame Mathieu used a cry like the cry of a cat. The people of the district, hearing it in the night, believed that it was the cat of Mother Angenoux, the Bête du bon Dieu. So the mournful sound that had frightened the servants of the Glandier had really come from a human throat, and a murmur of surprise ran round the benches, while some of the listeners began to laugh with relief.

She was also, Rouletabille declared, the black phantom that Daddy Jacques had seen flitting through the park on the night of the crime, and whom the old servant had taken for a ghost or for the Devil himself. He explained that this innocent secret had served to hide a far more terrible one, and that people had been looking in the wrong direction for months. Madame Mathieu hid her face in her shawl, and her shoulders shook, while her husband sat as still as a stone beside her.

The hands of the great clock above the president's head moved slowly toward half-past six, and the court, now utterly silent, waited with its eyes fixed upon the young man in the travelling coat. When the clock at last struck the half-hour, Rouletabille took out his watch, looked at it carefully, snapped it shut and put it back in his pocket. It was, in the opinion of everybody present, the longest minute that the court had ever known, and nobody remembered to breathe.

Then he turned toward the empty chair beside the witness stand, and in a ringing voice he named the murderer of the Yellow Room as Frédéric Larsan. The great detective, however, who had slipped quietly out of the court while the crowd was listening to the story of the tower, was no longer there to hear his own name pronounced. Only the empty chair remained, and it seemed to stare back at the crowd with a kind of silent mockery.

Rouletabille added that Larsan was not Larsan at all, but Ballmeyer, the greatest criminal of the age, who had deceived the police of more than one country for many years. The court broke into an uproar, the guards ran toward the doors, the spectators leapt up on the benches, and the president struck the table again and again with his hammer. Nobody in the whole building could hear a single word that anyone else was saying, and the noise went on for several minutes.

Ballmeyer, he continued when order had returned, had escaped from the police many times, changing his face and name as other men change their coats, so that no one had ever been able to describe him with any certainty. His boldest stroke of all had been to enter the Sûreté itself, which hunted him, and to work there under a name that was not his own. It was a mask, Rouletabille said, that no policeman would ever think of tearing off.

The president rang his bell again and again and called loudly for silence, threatening to clear the court, and little by little the noise fell and the crowd sank back into its seats. A great stillness settled on the hall, and all those hundreds of faces turned toward Rouletabille, eager to hear the rest of the strange tale. He smiled, took his pipe out of his pocket, and then remembered just in time where he was and put it back.

Rouletabille laid an iron peg on the table in front of the judges and asked them to look at it closely, turning it over in his fingers so that all could see the rust at its tip. It fitted exactly, he said, a hole that he had discovered in the wall beneath the terrace of the château. The president leaned forward in his high chair to examine it, and the judges on either side of him did the same.

Larsan, he told the court, had used this peg as a step to climb up the wall to the terrace, and from the terrace he could reach the window of the gallery without ever being seen from the court. It was a trick that only a very agile and a very daring man could have attempted. He had practised it, it seemed, more than once, and he had left the peg in its hole until it was needed again.

The detective had done it on the last night, when the whole household was running about the court with lanterns and carrying the dead keeper toward the lodge, and in all that confusion nobody noticed that he was missing. For several minutes the great Larsan had been absent, and no one had asked where he was. Rouletabille paused and let the silence of the court speak for itself, and not a single voice interrupted him.

Larsan had also slipped a sleeping drug into Rouletabille's drink at dinner, while pretending to fall asleep himself in his armchair, so that the one man in the house who watched him should be out of the way. That was why the young reporter could not be woken until Sainclair, in despair, threw a jug of cold water over his face. He had been outwitted by a cleverer man than himself, and he admitted it to the court quite frankly and without any shame.

Rouletabille now turned to the mystery of the gallery, which had puzzled the whole of France for weeks and had been called impossible by the most learned men of the Sûreté. The red-bearded man could not have escaped from the gallery, he explained, for there was no way out, and therefore, since he could not have gone, he had never gone away at all. His logic was beautifully simple, and as he spoke it, the faces in the court slowly began to change from doubt to understanding.

If the man had not escaped, then he must still have been in the gallery when the four men met at the crossing, and he had stood there among them in the lamplight. This meant that one of the four men who had run after the fugitive was the murderer himself. The court gasped aloud at the idea, and a woman in the front row cried out that it was impossible.

In two seconds, as he turned the corner out of sight of the others, Larsan had pulled off a false red beard and hidden it in the lining of his coat. Then he had joined the chase as the fourth pursuer, running in from the end of the gallery and shouting louder than any of the rest. It was a stroke of real genius, as Rouletabille was the first to admit, and it had deceived all of them.

Upon the table in front of the president, Rouletabille placed a pair of steel eye-glasses which had been found on the floor of Mathilde's sitting room on the night of the chase. They belonged to Larsan, who had dropped them in his flight, and they proved beyond all doubt that the detective had been in that room that night. The president examined them slowly in silence, and then he passed them to the clerk, who wrote down a long note.

Larsan had loved Mathilde Stangerson madly, Rouletabille said, with a love that was stronger than his reason, and he had followed her in secret for a long time without ever declaring himself. One day he had found a key which she had lost, and with that key he had been able to open the iron cabinet in the laboratory. The court listened breathlessly to this strange confession of the detective's heart, and some of the women were visibly moved.

He had stolen the papers of the old professor, which he could not use and had little reason to want. Later, in a moment of weakness or perhaps of remorse, he had put them all back on the floor of her sitting room, where the household found them the next morning. It was, said Rouletabille, the act of a man who was torn in two by his love and by his crimes, and he almost pitied him.

Rouletabille announced that the murderer had never been locked in the Yellow Room at midnight, and that the whole mystery had been wrongly set from the start. A silence fell over the court, for every person present had accepted the locked room as a fact. He asked them to forget, for a moment, everything that they had heard and read about the case since October.

The attack, he explained, had really happened about six o'clock in the evening, many hours before the cries were heard, when Mathilde had gone into her room alone while her father and old Jacques worked in the laboratory. At that hour nobody had thought to look for a murderer, and nobody would have found one. Her secret, which she had told to nobody, had done the rest, and it had kept her silent when she ought to have spoken.

The man had been hiding beneath her bed, with his heavy boots in his hand, and he had waited patiently until she was alone before leaping out and seizing her by the throat. She had struggled desperately, and in the struggle her throat had been marked by the fingers of the man who held her. It had been a few seconds of horror, and she had never forgotten them.

Mathilde, who had borrowed Jacques's revolver for exactly that reason, had managed to draw it and to fire, and the bullet had wounded his hand, which had left the red print on the wall as he tried to steady himself. The man had cried out in pain and had released her at once, and she had fallen back against the wall. It had been the only blow she had been able to strike, and it had been enough to save her life.

The wounded man fled through the hall window, leaving traces of blood on its blinds, and Mathilde, shaking, closed the window behind him and said nothing to anyone, because she was afraid and because she was keeping a secret. She locked herself into her room that night, as she had done before, and she took up her work again as though nothing had happened. Nobody in the great house, nor in the laboratory beside her, guessed what had passed in that quiet pavilion.

At midnight, alone in the locked room and exhausted by pain and fear, she had dreamed of the attack and cried out for help in her sleep, and in her terror she had overturned the little table by her bed. The revolver, which lay on it, had gone off, and Mathilde herself had struck her temple on the marble corner of the table as she fell. The two men in the laboratory had heard it all, and they had taken it for the sound of a murder in progress.

Larsan, who had needed a victim for the police, had stolen the boots and the cap of Daddy Jacques, and he had also ordered boots made exactly like Darzac's, so that his own tracks should point toward two innocent men. The cap, the heavy prints and the neat prints by the lake had therefore been his own work, from first to last. It had been a game of extraordinary skill, played by a man who knew every rule of the police.

With the false boots he had walked in the mud and left his neat prints beside the lake, and he had studied the habits of Darzac for months. He had wanted the police to suspect both men, and he had wanted, above all, to be the one who found the truth. Rouletabille spoke of him with a certain cold admiration, as one speaks of a very dangerous and very gifted opponent.

As a detective, Larsan had then cleared one of the suspects before accusing the other, so that nobody could say that he had been unfair or hasty. It was the game of a master criminal who used the law to play with the law, and for a time he had won every move, until a round-headed boy had followed the facts to the end. The president lowered his head and sighed deeply, and the whole court seemed to sigh with him as the explanation came to its end.

The trial was adjourned, and the next day Darzac was set free and Daddy Jacques was cleared of every suspicion, while Larsan, as everyone expected, could not be found anywhere. Rouletabille, who was not yet nineteen, became the hero of the hour, and the crowds cheered him in the streets of Versailles and carried him on their shoulders. He was only embarrassed by all the noise, and he asked quietly, with a shy smile, whether anybody had seen his pipe.

That night, on the train that carried them back to Paris, Sainclair soon fell asleep by the window, but before he did so Rouletabille told him that the lie about the yellow cane ought to have warned them both. A man who lies without reason about so small a thing, he said, has something very large to hide. The wheels rattled on through the dark countryside, and the carriage rocked gently from side to side like a cradle.

Larsan, Rouletabille went on, had not bought the cane for show but because his hand had been wounded and he needed a stick to lean on and to hide the injury. It was the wound that Mathilde's bullet had made, as she defended herself at six o'clock in the pavilion, and it had marked the criminal as plainly as a name. His own vanity, and his need to lean on that stick, had betrayed him in the end to a boy who watched everything.

The secret of Mathilde Stangerson, which could now be told, began long before, in Philadelphia, where she had lived with her father as a young girl. There she had fallen in love with a witty, graceful Frenchman who called himself Jean Roussel, and who spoke beautifully and made her laugh. To a lonely young woman in a foreign city he had seemed like a prince out of a story, and she had thought herself the happiest girl in America.

When Monsieur Stangerson discovered that the man was a swindler and refused his consent, the young woman, indignant and in love, ran away to be married in secret. The couple lived for some time in the town of Louisville in a little house with a garden, where they were poor but happy. For a few months she believed that she had found perfect happiness in the little house, which was called the Presbytery and stood at the end of a quiet street with a garden in front of it.

One morning, however, the police knocked at the door of the little house to arrest her husband, and in that terrible moment she learned that he was not Jean Roussel at all but the notorious criminal Ballmeyer. The man she had loved and married was a hunted criminal, and every word that he had told her had been a lie. She stood in the doorway of the little house, quite unable to speak, while the police took him away.

Heartbroken and ashamed, Mathilde returned to her father, who never knew where she had been or what had happened to her, and she hid the truth from him as one hides a wound. She worked harder than ever in the laboratory at his side, believing that her devotion to science would atone for her disobedience. In this way the years passed quietly by, and nobody in the old château, least of all her father, suspected that she carried so heavy a burden.

After some years a rumour reached her that Ballmeyer was dead, and Mathilde dared to hope that her past was buried with him. When at last she agreed to marry Robert Darzac, to whom she had told everything, she believed that she was beginning a new life, without shadows and without fear. Darzac, who loved her, had heard her story with great kindness and had promised to stand beside her whatever should come.

Then the man she had thought dead wrote her a letter that ended with the sentence Rouletabille had overheard: the presbytery had lost nothing of its charm, nor the garden its brightness. That was the name of the little house in Louisville where they had lived together, and she understood at once what it meant. The words fell on her like a blow, and from that moment she knew no peace by day or by night.

In the letter he threatened that if she married another man he would destroy her father's life work and would reveal everything to the old professor, who knew nothing. Mathilde, who loved her father more than she feared the criminal, chose to suffer in silence and to hide the truth from everybody, even at the cost of her own life. That was the strange sorrow that Rouletabille had seen in her eyes, and that nobody else in the whole house had understood.

Mathilde slowly recovered, and Robert Darzac, free and happy again, hoped that careful nursing would one day give her back her peace of mind. The mystery of the Yellow Room had been solved by a boy of eighteen, who had followed reason to the end and had still protected the secret that had cost her so dearly. Two months later Sainclair found his friend alone on a bench in the Palace of Justice, looking sad, and Rouletabille would only sigh that he was thinking of the perfume of the lady in black.
